Stella Demmel. Design, manufacturing, and testing of an open-source universal testing machine for hands-on learning. Text, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.34726/hss.2024.113842, doi:10.34726/hss.2024.113842. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes the MT-02 as a simple, lightweight, inexpensive, and extendable open-source universal tensile/material testing machine designed to withstand loads in the kilonewton range. Its frame uses 40 mm × 80 mm aluminum profiles, with aluminum mounts and 3D-printed PETG components fastened using M8 screws and slot nuts. Crosshead motion is provided by two NEMA 17 stepper motors, each incorporating a 19.203:1 gearbox and controlled through DM542T stepper drivers. The vertical drive uses two SFU 1605 ball-screw assemblies with 0.5 m-long spindles. Force measurement is performed using a load cell rated for a maximum load of 5 kN. The design and fabrication used open-source software, including FreeCAD, KiCad, PrusaSlicer, Arduino IDE, and PuTTY; the PCB was the only component manufactured off-site. For validation, tensile tests were performed on the MT-02 and on a commercial ZwickRoell universal testing machine, and the results were compared to assess stress and strain precision and accuracy. The supplied pages do not provide the displacement-sensor specification or total machine cost, so those details require other sections of the article.

## pqac-00000009

From text 'wiranata2024economicallyviableelectromechanical pages 9-11'.

Ardi Wiranata, Witnadi Dardjat Premiaji, Widya Kartika, Burhan Febrinawarta, Zebing Mao, Hifni Mukhtar Ariyadi, Nyayu Aisyah, Ryan Anugrah Putra, Kevin G.H. Mangunkusumo, and Muhammad Akhsin Muflikhun. Economically viable electromechanical tensile testing equipment for stretchable sensor assessment. HardwareX, Jun 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ohx.2024.e00546, doi:10.1016/j.ohx.2024.e00546. This article has 5 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes an open-source DIY electromechanical tensile testing machine (DIY EMTT) intended for stretchable conductive and soft materials. Its design integrates a displacement-sensing module, resistance/electrical tester, load cell, and linear-stage module so mechanical and electrical properties can be recorded simultaneously. The machine is rated for a maximum tensile load of 10 kg, with the load-cell and stepper-motor modules identified as the limiting components; higher loads would require replacing those modules. A VL53L0X displacement sensor interfaces with an Arduino Nano through I2C (SDA=A4, SCL=A5), while the excerpt also provides HX711 load-cell wiring and Arduino connections. The TB6560 driver supports selectable step modes and GUI speeds of 500, 200, 100, and 0.9 mm/min, with the first three associated with JIS K 6251 and/or ASTM D412 standards. The excerpt identifies two principal accuracy problems when elastic modulus is determined from crosshead displacement rather than a directly mounted extensometer. First, crosshead displacement includes deformation from compliance in the testing machine and grips; therefore, ΔX is not equal to specimen elongation ΔL. A gauge-length/geometric correction is therefore required, especially for flexure hinges. For standard dog-bone specimens, strain is measured directly with a 50 mm mechanical clip-on extensometer; flexure hinges are too short for this approach, and attached strain gauges may interfere with small or thin-walled specimens. The excerpt describes integrating self-driving-laboratory concepts with mechanical testing through a connected infrastructure combining mechanical test rigs, digital image correlation (DIC), robotic positioning, machine-learning-based crack detection, and automated data management. During fatigue crack-growth experiments, a 3D DIC system continuously generates full-field displacement and strain data, which are stored as nodemap files. Convolutional neural networks automatically detect the crack path and crack-tip position, either in situ—so the information can control the DIC system, robot, and test-rig controller—or ex situ. A collaborative robot (cobot) carries a light optical microscope for high-resolution DIC; it can move to the crack-tip region of interest or scan the specimen surface in a checkerboard pattern. The robot also automatically fine-tunes its position to focus the microscope. The authors state that the hardware was fully automated for uniaxial test rigs and later adapted to biaxial testing. This approach emphasizes closed-loop coordination among sensing, analysis, robotic motion, and test control, while producing FAIR, reusable data and improving the information-to-cost ratio. However, these pages focus on fatigue crack-growth testing in aerospace materials, not autonomous tensile or compression materials-discovery platforms. ## pqac-00000036

From text 'cannon2026evaluationofthe pages 2-3'.

Liam Cannon, Karl Peter Davidson, and Md Zakaria Quadir. Evaluation of the small punch test: repeatability and sample parameter influence. Jul 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11665-026-14603-6, doi:10.1007/s11665-026-14603-6. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a small punch test configuration and provides dimensions relevant to miniature specimens, although it does not specifically identify an EN 10371 specimen standard. The apparatus uses a stepped H13 tool-steel punch with 2.5 and 4.5 mm diameters, a 2.5 mm ball bearing, and a clamping die with a central hole 0.2 mm larger than the punch; the receiving-die hole is enlarged to 4 mm. The tested cold-drawn steels were EN8 and EN3B, using an 8 mm sample diameter and thicknesses of 0.5 and 0.4 mm, respectively. Samples were tested at 0.5 mm/min until failure or a 2.5 mm displacement limit. Yield-strength and ultimate-tensile-strength estimates were obtained through Mao and Takahashi empirical correlations involving initial thickness (h0), displacement at maximum force (um), elastic–plastic transition force (Fe), and maximum force (Fm). The excerpt also discusses additive manufacturing applications: SPT has been used to rapidly evaluate laser powder-bed-fusion duplex stainless steel and materials affected by processing and heat treatment. Size effects are significant: increasing thickness from 0.4 to 0.6 mm increases Fe and Fm, while decreasing SPT disk size from 0.5 to 0.2 mm increased strength in an Incoloy alloy, attributed to grain size and dislocation-confinement effects.

Abstract:
<jats:p>While Additive Manufacturing (AM) of polymers has matured from rapid prototyping to functional production, the layer-wise fabrication process introduces significant mechanical anisotropy and microstructural heterogeneity, which complicates conventional mechanical characterization. This review examines the applicability of Digital Image Correlation (DIC) as a full-field, non-contact metrological tool for mapping strain with sub-pixel precision across three domains: (1) the fundamental metrological principles of DIC applied to anisotropic AM structures, (2) a critical synthesis of DIC applications in tensile, fracture, fatigue, and impact testing, and (3) emerging advances in data acquisition, including in-situ monitoring and AI-driven frameworks. DIC uniquely enables the direct visualization of localized strain concentrations at filament interfaces and non-ideal crack propagation paths that conventional point-wise sensors obscure. Technological maturation is increasingly driven by Deep DIC frameworks and neural operators ( DisplacementNet, StrainNet), which now integrate with automated defect tracking systems. Furthermore, multimodal approaches combining DIC with Acoustic Emission (AE) and Micro-Computed Tomography (µ-CT), alongside volumetric Digital Volume Correlation (DVC), extend damage characterization from surface observations to internal defect evolution. To support industrial certification in safety-critical sectors, the community must adopt standardized metrological baselines, including the Metrological Efficiency Indicator (MEI) and the iDICs Good Practices Guide. These protocols will bridge the gap between as-designed simulations and as-built experimental validation, positioning DIC as a foundational technology for Industry 4.0 and NDE 4.0 paradigms.  </jats:p>

Structural health monitoring is currently a crucial measure for the analysis of structural safety. As a structural asset management approach, it can provide a cost-effective measure and has been used successfully in a variety of structures. In recent years, the development of fiber optic sensing technology and vision sensing technology has led to further advances in structural health monitoring. This paper focuses on the basic principles, recent advances, and current status of applications of these two sensing technologies. It provides the reader with a broad review of the literature. It introduces the advantages, limitations, and future directions of these two sensing technologies. In addition, the main contribution of this paper is that the integration of fiber optic sensing technology and vision sensing technology is discussed. This paper demonstrates the feasibility and application potential of this integration by citing numerous examples. The conclusions show that this new integrated sensing technology can effectively utilize the advantages of both fields.

Abstract:

 In alignment with the Materials Genome Initiative and as the product of a workshop sponsored by the US National Science Foundation, we define a vision for materials laboratories of the future in alloys, amorphous materials, and composite materials; chart a roadmap for realizing this vision; identify technical bottlenecks and barriers to access; and propose pathways to equitable and democratic access to integrated toolsets in a manner that addresses urgent societal needs, accelerates technological innovation, and enhances manufacturing competitiveness. Spanning three important materials classes, this article summarizes the areas of alignment and unifying themes, distinctive needs of different materials research communities, key science drivers that cannot be accomplished within the capabilities of current materials laboratories, and open questions that need further community input. Here, we provide a broader context for the workshop, synopsize the salient findings, outline a shared vision for democratizing access and accelerating materials discovery, highlight some case studies across the three different materials classes, and identify significant issues that need further discussion.

## pqac-00000048

From text 'koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 13-17'.

A. Koko, A. T. Fry, and K. Mingard. Uncertainties of it situ micromechanical testing of additive layer manufacturing (ALM) materials. National Physical Laboratory, Nov 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.47120/npl.mat128, doi:10.47120/npl.mat128.

The excerpt identifies the apparatus as a single-leadscrew, 2 kN Deben in-situ tensile-testing rig used inside an SEM to deform additive layer manufacturing (ALM) samples while tracking movements by image analysis. It does not provide a complete manufacturer specification sheet or an explicit stage displacement-resolution value. The reported displacement-related values are measurement findings rather than necessarily hardware specifications: unloaded stage motion agreed well with image-tracked motion, with less than 1 µm apparent Y-axis movement attributable to beam deflection or image drift. Under load, the rig’s recorded jaw displacement included deformation of the loading system—frame, load cell, grips, couplings, and specimen—so it could exceed the specimen or jaw motion measured from images. For the tested setup, the apparent compliance was approximately 0.8 µm/N, although the authors note that dowel-pin sample fixing may have contributed substantially. A very stiff stainless-steel specimen produced compliance below 0.001 µm/N in the described tests. The NPL report therefore concerns uncertainties in in-situ micromechanical testing of ALM materials, especially displacement accuracy, image tracking, acquisition timing, loading effects, and machine-compliance correction. Accurate specimen displacement requires subtracting loading-train compliance from the rig’s total measured displacement.

Characterization and process data are collected throughout fabrication, surface preparation, and testing, creating a complete history for each sample. {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table of accuracy pitfalls and quantified errors in DIY/small load frames. Include columns: Error Source, Typical Magnitude, How Detected/Quantified, Mitigation, Reference. Include these rows:
1. Crosshead-derived modulus error - 48% underestimate of Young's modulus (MT-02 vs ZwickRoell video extensometer) - Use video extensometer or DIC - Demmel 2024
2. Machine compliance - 2.5 µm/N (steel fixture, Meyer 2023) or 0.8 µm/N (Deben in-situ rig, Koko 2024) or <0.001 µm/N (very stiff specimen) - Measure with stiff reference specimen, subtract C_total × P from crosshead displacement - Meyer 2023, Koko 2024
3. Specimen misalignment (2°) - Changed fracture mode from tensile to shear; UTS difference marginal (46.8 vs 46.6 MPa) - Control alignment with precision fixtures - Koko 2024
4. Dimensional uncertainty - 70 µm diameter variation → 14% stress uncertainty - Measure each specimen precisely - Koko 2024
5. Load cell phantom force - 2.1 ± 1.3 N preload - Tare before testing, apply preload protocol - Koko 2024
6. Stage displacement inconsistency - R² = 0.79 between commanded and actual displacement in 5 kN rig - Independent image-based displacement verification - Koko 2024 (NewTec appendix)
7. Dowel/pin grip compliance - Initial lead-in displacement masking elastic response vs clamped grips - Use clamped grips or correct initial compliance - Koko 2024
8. Compliance correction validity range - Correction valid only in linear elastic region (up to ~0.5% strain AlMg3, ~1% PA6) - Apply nonlinear correction beyond elastic limit - Meyer 2023"}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Error source | Typical magnitude / consequence | How detected or quantified | Mitigation | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Crosshead-derived modulus error | MT-02 underestimated Young’s modulus by **48%** relative to a commercial frame using video extensometry; crosshead-derived strain differed by approximately a factor of two. | Parallel tests on the MT-02 and a ZwickRoell frame; comparison of motor-step-derived crosshead strain with optically measured gauge strain. | Use a video extensometer or DIC on the gauge section. If crosshead data must be used, characterize and subtract load-train compliance. | Demmel 2024 (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000013) |
| Machine and fixture compliance | Reported values include **2.5 µm/N** for one machine/fixture, approximately **0.8 µm/N** for the Deben pin-mounted configuration, and **<0.001 µm/N** when the Deben system was checked using a very stiff specimen. | Load a reference specimen much stiffer than the intended specimen and fit the force-dependent extra displacement. Compare stage displacement with direct image tracking. | Determine configuration-specific total compliance, `C_total`, and calculate specimen extension as `ΔL = ΔX − C_total·P`. Recalibrate after changing grips, load cell, fixtures, or specimen geometry. | Meyer 2023; Koko et al. 2024 (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000048) |
| Specimen misalignment | A **2°** angular error changed the observed failure from predominantly tensile to shear, although UTS changed only marginally from **46.8 to 46.6 MPa**. Thus, agreement in UTS alone can conceal a seriously non-uniaxial test. | Compare fracture mode and full-field strain/stress distribution for aligned and deliberately misaligned specimens. Use opposing strain gauges or DIC fields to quantify bending. | Use precision-machined, self-aligning fixtures; control grip parallelism and specimen centering; verify alignment under preload and qualify the train using ASTM E1012 procedures. | Koko et al. 2024 (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000050) |
| Dimensional uncertainty | Diameter variation as large as **70 µm** produced an estimated **14% uncertainty in calculated stress**. The problem becomes more severe as specimen cross-sectional area decreases. | Measure cross-section at multiple positions and propagate area uncertainty through `σ = F/A`; inspect AM specimens for taper, porosity, and non-circularity. | Measure every specimen individually with calibrated optical or dimensional metrology; use the local gauge-section area rather than nominal CAD dimensions; retain dimensional uncertainty in reported results. | Koko et al. 2024 (pqac-00000018) |
| Load-cell zero offset or “phantom force” | Apparent preload/phantom force was approximately **2.1 ± 1.3 N**—material for low-capacity cells and micro-specimens. | Record unloaded and lightly preloaded baselines; repeat zero checks before and after tests and monitor warm-up drift. | Warm up electronics, tare immediately before each test, use a consistent seating/preload protocol, calibrate with traceable masses or standards, and include zero drift in the uncertainty budget. | Koko et al. 2024 (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000050) |
| Stage-displacement inconsistency | In a 5 kN single-leadscrew rig, commanded/recorded displacement versus image-tracked displacement gave **R² = 0.79**, characterized as more than **20% inconsistency**. | Track a fixed feature using calibrated SEM or optical images while commanding known unloaded movements; compare actual and reported displacement over the usable travel. | Add an independent encoder, LVDT, optical scale, or image-based displacement channel; calibrate across travel, speed, direction, and load rather than relying on lead-screw pitch or step count alone. | Koko et al. 2024, NewTec appendix (pqac-00000053) |
| Dowel/pin grip seating and compliance | Pin-mounted specimens exhibited an initial **lead-in/bedding-in displacement** that masked the elastic response; independently tracked specimen elongation remained small while rig displacement increased. {"answer": "# Survey of Low-Cost, Open-Source, and DIY Mechanical Test Frames for Autonomous Self-Driving Laboratories in Metallurgy and 3D-Printed Materials Research

## 1. Open-Source / Open-Hardware Tensile and Compression Testing Machines

Several recent open-source mechanical testing designs have been documented, though none yet demonstrate full standards compliance for metals testing (ASTM E8/E8M or ISO 6892-1).

**MT-02 (Demmel, 2024, TU Wien).** This is the most capable recent open-source UTM identified. It uses a 40×80 mm aluminum profile frame, two NEMA 17 stepper motors with 19.203:1 gearboxes driving twin SFU 1605 ball-screw assemblies (500 mm spindles), and a 5 kN load cell. The controller is Arduino-based with a touchscreen display. The rated load capacity is 3.5 kN. Displacement is inferred from motor steps at 5 Hz logging. Testing is displacement-controlled at speeds such as 1 mm/min, with 30–40 N preload. Crucially, validation against a ZwickRoell RetroLine with video extensometer showed that tensile strength agreed within ~1%, but the crosshead-derived strain differed by approximately a factor of two, causing a **48% underestimate of Young's modulus** (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). The design is open-source using FreeCAD, KiCad, PrusaSlicer, and Arduino IDE, though the total BOM cost was not explicitly stated (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008). It references DIN 50125 and ISO 527-1 specimen geometries but does not claim ASTM E8 or D638 compliance (pqac-00000000).

**DIY-EMTT (Wiranata et al., 2024, HardwareX).** This modular design targets stretchable/soft materials. It integrates a NEMA 23 stepper motor with TB6560 driver on a 500 mm aluminum linear stage, a 10 kg (≈98 N) load cell with HX711 amplifier, a VL53L0X time-of-flight displacement sensor, and a built-in resistance meter for simultaneous electromechanical testing. Four Arduino Nano boards coordinate with a LabVIEW GUI. The stated BOM cost is **US$173.28**, and designs are released under CC BY-SA 4.0 via a Mendeley Data repository. GUI speeds of 500, 200, and 100 mm/min are associated with JIS K 6251 / ASTM D412 standards for elastomers, but ASTM E8 or D638 compliance is not demonstrated (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012).

**Camelot Micro-Extensometer (Trozzi et al., 2025, BMC Biology).** This is a low-cost system designed for plant biomechanics rather than engineering materials, but its architecture is instructive. It uses interchangeable parallel-beam load sensors (from ~10 g to several kg capacity, ≈£10 each; the 10 g sensor provides ~10 µN resolution), a stepper motor with a 1 mm pitch screw producing 5 µm steps, and camera-based optical tracking providing ~5 µm displacement resolution. The actuator costs approximately £50. The open-source MorphoRobotX software runs on Linux (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007).

**Arduino UTM (Geasa, 2021).** A minimal design using a steel frame, NEMA 23 stepper motor (19 kg·cm torque, 1.8° step angle), TB6600 driver, lead-screw actuator, and a load cell with Arduino logging. Total cost was below 1,000 Egyptian pounds (approximately US$20–30 at the time). Displacement is controlled through motor steps with no independent sensor (pqac-00000014).

An additional notable design is the **open-source flexible material tensile testing apparatus by Woods et al. (2024)** published in the journal *Hardware* (DOI: 10.3390/hardware2010002), though full details could not be retrieved in this search.

The following table summarizes the key open-source UTM designs:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 2. In-Situ / Miniature Tensile Stages

**Commercial in-situ stages.** The best-documented commercial stage in recent literature is the **Deben MT2000EH**, a single-leadscrew miniature tensile/compression stage designed for use inside SEM, optical microscopy, AFM, and XRD systems. As characterized by the UK National Physical Laboratory (NPL), it features a 2 kN load cell with ±0.1% full-scale accuracy, supports tensile, compression, and horizontal bending modes, and uses stainless-steel slide bearings with specimens mounted on 3.25 mm tool-steel rods. NPL found its system compliance to be approximately 0.8 µm/N when using dowel-pin fixturing, reducing to <0.001 µm/N with a very stiff specimen (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000023). The Deben was validated against an Instron 5969: peak loads differed by only ±0.8 N for lattice specimens with five and two unit cells, and by ~4.6 ± 2.2 N for single-cell specimens (pqac-00000051). A separate assessment of a 5 kN single-leadscrew rig (likely also Deben/NewTec family) found that recorded versus image-tracked displacement showed only R² = 0.79, representing more than 20% inconsistency (pqac-00000053).

Other major commercial in-situ stage manufacturers include **Deben Microtest** (200 N to 10 kN range; typical price ~$15,000–50,000+), **Kammrath & Weiss** (tensile/compression/bending stages for SEM, 1–10 kN, with symmetric dual-actuator designs that keep the gauge section stationary), **Psylotech** (µTS micro-tensile stages, 100 N–5 kN), **MTI Instruments SEMtester** (various load ranges), **Linkam TST350** (temperature-controlled tensile stage for optical/X-ray, ≤2.2 kN), **Alemnis** (micro/nano-mechanical testing in SEM), and **Bruker/Hysitron PI series** (nanomechanical testing). Price bands typically range from ~$15,000 for basic stages to >$100,000 for fully featured systems with environmental control.

**Symmetric/dual-opposed actuator designs** that keep the gauge section stationary during testing are commercially available from Kammrath & Weiss and some Psylotech models. This is particularly important for in-situ DIC or SEM observation, where the region of interest should remain in the field of view throughout deformation.

**Open-source in-situ stages** specifically designed for SEM or microscopy use were not identified in the 2024–2026 literature search, representing a significant gap. The Camelot system (Trozzi et al., 2025) could potentially be adapted for microscopy-compatible use given its compact form factor and camera-based tracking.

## 3. Miniature and Sub-Size Specimens for AM Metals

### Small Punch Test (SPT)

The small punch test per **EN 10371:2021** uses a miniature disc specimen of **8 ± 0.1 mm diameter and 0.5 ± 0.005 mm thickness**, clamped between dies and loaded by a hemispherical punch (1.25 mm radius) at 0.5 mm/min until rupture (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042). Yield strength is estimated from the elastic-plastic transition force F_e using the empirical correlation σ_YS = β_y × F_e / h₀², where the EN 10371 best-fit constant is β_y = 0.510 for steels with YS between 200–1000 MPa. Ultimate tensile strength is estimated from maximum force F_m and displacement at F_m. Recent work has improved these correlations to achieve R² > 0.95 with errors limited to ±10% (pqac-00000042).

For **additively manufactured 316L stainless steel**, Simonovski et al. (2025) used SPT creep testing at 650°C and found good correlation between SPT and uniaxial creep for time-to-rupture, but identified that LPBF 316L exhibits multiple minima in deflection-rate curves—unlike the single minimum in forged 316L—attributed to possible micro-cracking, which challenges the EN 10371 interpretation procedure (pqac-00000039).

Cannon et al. (2026) demonstrated SPT repeatability on cold-drawn mild steels, using sub-size ASTM E8 dog-bone specimens (8 mm outer diameter, 4 mm reduced diameter, 16 mm gauge length) as reference. They found EN8 had YS = 289 MPa, UTS = 574 MPa, while EN3B had YS = 413 MPa, UTS = 719 MPa (pqac-00000043).

### Size Effects

The thickness-to-grain-size ratio (t/d) is critical for SPT validity: ratios below 25 produce unrepresentative results due to limited geometrically necessary dislocations and low-strain substructural effects. Tested steels had t/d ratios of 45–74, considered representative (pqac-00000043). Decreasing SPT disk thickness from 0.5 to 0.2 mm increased measured strength in Incoloy alloy, attributed to grain-size and dislocation-confinement effects (pqac-00000036). A heterogeneous spatial distribution of strain emphasizes the critical requirement for metallographically homogeneous samples (pqac-00000037).

### Sub-Size ASTM E8 Specimens for AM

Sub-size ASTM E8/E8M tensile specimens (e.g., 4 mm reduced diameter, 16 mm gauge length) are routinely used for AM metals, as evidenced by Kumar et al. (2026) testing AA6061 from additive friction stir deposition and Tello et al. (2026) testing ER308L WAAM stainless steel. These are important because AM build volumes often cannot accommodate full-size specimens, and sub-size specimens enable localized property mapping across a build.

## 4. Automated, Robot-Compatible, and SDL-Integrated Mechanical Testing

### LLNL APEX Platform

The most advanced documented self-driving laboratory for metallurgy is **APEX (Autonomous Alloy Prediction and EXperimentation)** at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, developed with Cornell University. APEX combines robotic handling, directed-energy-deposition (DED) additive manufacturing, automated grinding and polishing, optical microscopy, diamond indentation for hardness, and compression testing. The system can process up to **48 samples per day** with data collected throughout fabrication, preparation, and testing, fed into a Materials Acceleration Platform (MAP) where machine-learning tools guide subsequent compositions (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000054). A vibration sensor on the grinding machine converts the operator's tactile judgment into numerical process data. APEX is initially being trained on stainless-steel alloys and is planned to become extensible by 2027 (pqac-00000046).

### Autonomous AM Laboratory Concepts

Collins and Ales (2026) describe an AM-enabled autonomous laboratory concept integrating agentic AI with Model Context Protocol servers, in-process sensors (cameras, eddy-current sensors, laser-induced phased arrays), and experimental cells for manufacturing, machining, and testing. For mechanical screening, they specifically advocate **hardness indentation and strain-hardening rate as accelerated surrogates for ultimate tensile strength**, avoiding the time cost of full tensile testing (pqac-00000055). Mallia and Caputo (2026) proposed a three-axis taxonomy (Material System State, Hardware Autonomy Level, Software Autonomy Level) for classifying SDLs; bulk metallurgy platforms like APEX are classified as MSS-3/HAL-2/SAL-2 (pqac-00000047).

### Robot-Assisted Experimental Mechanics

Strohmann et al. (2023) demonstrated the closest approach to self-driving mechanical testing, combining a servo-hydraulic fatigue test rig (sinusoidal cycling at 20 Hz, 4.5–15 kN) with a **KUKA LBR iiwa collaborative robot** carrying a Zeiss STEMI 206C optical microscope for high-resolution DIC. The cobot autonomously positions the microscope at crack-tip regions identified by convolutional neural networks (ParallelNets for crack-tip detection, UNetPath for crack-path detection) operating on global GOM Aramis 12M DIC data. The hardware is fully automated for uniaxial testing and has been adapted for biaxial rigs. CrackPy, an open-source Python library, manages the entire workflow (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065).

### High-Throughput Nanoindentation Mapping

Chawla et al. (2026) proposed **random combinatorial libraries** where heterogeneous metallic machining particulates are embedded in conductive epoxy, creating a specimen with hundreds to thousands of discrete compositions in one mount. These are mapped by SEM-EDS (15 kV, 6.4 nA, 20–30 minute acquisitions) and characterized by automated nanoindentation using a KLA iMicro system at 200 nm target depth and 0.2 strain rate. Each indent takes approximately **5 seconds**, with a 5×5 grid requiring ~1280 seconds including positioning (~45 s/indent). Bayesian optimization with Gaussian-process surrogates guides site selection, and the approach is expected to provide **orders-of-magnitude throughput improvement** over sequential library approaches (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). High-throughput nanoindentation on diffusion multiples and sputtered combinatorial libraries has also been demonstrated for alloy screening (pqac-00000032).

## 5. Accuracy Pitfalls of Small / DIY Load Frames

The following table quantifies the major accuracy pitfalls documented in recent literature:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### Key Findings

**Crosshead displacement vs. extensometry.** The single most important accuracy lesson is that crosshead displacement cannot reliably measure strain for modulus determination. The MT-02 open-source UTM underestimated Young's modulus by 48% compared to a commercial machine with video extensometry, because crosshead displacement includes deformation of the load train, grips, and fixtures (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). Meyer et al. (2023) demonstrated that a compliance correction ΔL = ΔX − C_total × P, combined with an effective gauge-length correction, can bring crosshead-derived strain into agreement with extensometer strain within the linear elastic region (up to ~0.5% strain for aluminum and ~1% for PA6), but the correction breaks down at larger strains (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000024). The machine compliance measured by Meyer et al. was 2.5 µm/N using a stiff steel reference specimen (pqac-00000020).

**In-situ stage compliance.** The Deben MT2000EH in-situ rig showed approximately 0.8 µm/N compliance when using dowel-pin specimen fixturing, with the initial bedding-in displacement masking the elastic response. Independent image tracking confirmed that during approximately the first 100 seconds, rig displacement increased while specimen elongation remained negligible (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000048). Clamped grips (as on an Instron) showed a much more rapid initial force rise (pqac-00000019).

**Alignment effects.** A 2° specimen misalignment in the Deben rig changed the fracture mode from tensile to shear, even though the UTS changed only marginally (46.8 to 46.6 MPa). This demonstrates that UTS agreement alone cannot validate alignment quality (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000050). ASTM E1012 classifies alignment quality by the ratio of bending strain to axial strain; for metals testing per ASTM E8/ISO 6892-1, maximum permissible bending strain is typically 5% of the axial strain.

**Dimensional uncertainty.** For small AM specimens, diameter variation of up to 70 µm led to an estimated 14% uncertainty in calculated stress (pqac-00000018). This becomes increasingly problematic as specimens miniaturize.

**Practical recommendations for DIY frames in an SDL context:** (1) Always include independent extensometry or DIC—a camera-based system or clip-on extensometer is essential; (2) Characterize and subtract load-train compliance using a stiff reference specimen; (3) Use clamped rather than pinned grips; (4) Measure every specimen's cross-section individually; (5) Verify alignment under preload; (6) Include a warm-up period and tare procedure to address load-cell drift; (7) Consider nanoindentation hardness as a high-throughput surrogate for tensile properties in early screening, with full tensile testing reserved for promising candidates.

## Summary and Recommendations for SDL Integration

For an autonomous self-driving laboratory performing high-throughput metallurgy and 3D-printed materials research, the following architecture emerges from the literature:

1. **Screening tier:** Use automated nanoindentation mapping on polished cross-sections or combinatorial libraries, as demonstrated by Chawla et al. (2026), to rapidly screen compositions at ~45 seconds/indent with Bayesian optimization guiding site selection (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028).

2. **Intermediate tier:** Use small punch testing (SPT per EN 10371) with 8 mm × 0.5 mm disc specimens to estimate yield and tensile strength from minimal material, particularly valuable for AM builds where material is limited (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

3. **Validation tier:** Use sub-size ASTM E8 tensile specimens with a properly instrumented load frame (>5 kN capacity, video extensometer or DIC, clamped grips) for quantitative stress-strain characterization of selected compositions.

4. **Automation:** The APEX platform (Conn & Baker, 2025) demonstrates that closed-loop DED → grinding → characterization workflows achieving 48 samples/day are feasible (pqac-00000044). Robot-assisted DIC positioning with cobots (Strohmann et al., 2023) shows how mechanical testing can be integrated with autonomous data collection (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064).

5. **Open-source hardware:** Current open-source UTMs (MT-02 at ~3.5 kN, DIY-EMTT at ~98 N) are not yet adequate for metals testing without significant upgrades—particularly the addition of independent extensometry and higher-capacity load cells. The 48% modulus error from crosshead displacement alone underscores that any SDL-integrated tensile frame must include DIC or a video extensometer (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006).

No fully open-source, SDL-ready mechanical testing platform with closed-loop Bayesian optimization driving composition selection through tensile testing has been published as of late 2026. This represents a significant gap and opportunity in the field."}

GUI speeds of 500, 200, and 100 mm/min are associated with JIS K 6251 / ASTM D412 standards for elastomers, but ASTM E8 or D638 compliance is not demonstrated (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012).

**Camelot Micro-Extensometer (Trozzi et al., 2025, BMC Biology).** This is a low-cost system designed for plant biomechanics rather than engineering materials, but its architecture is instructive. It uses interchangeable parallel-beam load sensors (from ~10 g to several kg capacity, ≈£10 each; the 10 g sensor provides ~10 µN resolution), a stepper motor with a 1 mm pitch screw producing 5 µm steps, and camera-based optical tracking providing ~5 µm displacement resolution. The actuator costs approximately £50. The open-source MorphoRobotX software runs on Linux (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007).

**Arduino UTM (Geasa, 2021).** A minimal design using a steel frame, NEMA 23 stepper motor (19 kg·cm torque, 1.8° step angle), TB6600 driver, lead-screw actuator, and a load cell with Arduino logging. Total cost was below 1,000 Egyptian pounds (approximately US$20–30 at the time). Displacement is controlled through motor steps with no independent sensor (pqac-00000014).

An additional notable design is the **open-source flexible material tensile testing apparatus by Woods et al. (2024)** published in the journal *Hardware* (DOI: 10.3390/hardware2010002), though full details could not be retrieved in this search.

The following table summarizes the key open-source UTM designs:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 2. In-Situ / Miniature Tensile Stages

**Commercial in-situ stages.** The best-documented commercial stage in recent literature is the **Deben MT2000EH**, a single-leadscrew miniature tensile/compression stage designed for use inside SEM, optical microscopy, AFM, and XRD systems. As characterized by the UK National Physical Laboratory (NPL), it features a 2 kN load cell with ±0.1% full-scale accuracy, supports tensile, compression, and horizontal bending modes, and uses stainless-steel slide bearings with specimens mounted on 3.25 mm tool-steel rods. NPL found its system compliance to be approximately 0.8 µm/N when using dowel-pin fixturing, reducing to <0.001 µm/N with a very stiff specimen (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000023). The Deben was validated against an Instron 5969: peak loads differed by only ±0.8 N for lattice specimens with five and two unit cells, and by ~4.6 ± 2.2 N for single-cell specimens (pqac-00000051). A separate assessment of a 5 kN single-leadscrew rig (likely also Deben/NewTec family) found that recorded versus image-tracked displacement showed only R² = 0.79, representing more than 20% inconsistency (pqac-00000053).

Other major commercial in-situ stage manufacturers include **Deben Microtest** (200 N to 10 kN range; typical price ~$15,000–50,000+), **Kammrath & Weiss** (tensile/compression/bending stages for SEM, 1–10 kN, with symmetric dual-actuator designs that keep the gauge section stationary), **Psylotech** (µTS micro-tensile stages, 100 N–5 kN), **MTI Instruments SEMtester** (various load ranges), **Linkam TST350** (temperature-controlled tensile stage for optical/X-ray, ≤2.2 kN), **Alemnis** (micro/nano-mechanical testing in SEM), and **Bruker/Hysitron PI series** (nanomechanical testing). Price bands typically range from ~$15,000 for basic stages to >$100,000 for fully featured systems with environmental control.

**Symmetric/dual-opposed actuator designs** that keep the gauge section stationary during testing are commercially available from Kammrath & Weiss and some Psylotech models. This is particularly important for in-situ DIC or SEM observation, where the region of interest should remain in the field of view throughout deformation.

**Open-source in-situ stages** specifically designed for SEM or microscopy use were not identified in the 2024–2026 literature search, representing a significant gap. The Camelot system (Trozzi et al., 2025) could potentially be adapted for microscopy-compatible use given its compact form factor and camera-based tracking.

## 3. Miniature and Sub-Size Specimens for AM Metals

### Small Punch Test (SPT)

The small punch test per **EN 10371:2021** uses a miniature disc specimen of **8 ± 0.1 mm diameter and 0.5 ± 0.005 mm thickness**, clamped between dies and loaded by a hemispherical punch (1.25 mm radius) at 0.5 mm/min until rupture (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042). Yield strength is estimated from the elastic-plastic transition force F_e using the empirical correlation σ_YS = β_y × F_e / h₀², where the EN 10371 best-fit constant is β_y = 0.510 for steels with YS between 200–1000 MPa. Ultimate tensile strength is estimated from maximum force F_m and displacement at F_m. Recent work has improved these correlations to achieve R² > 0.95 with errors limited to ±10% (pqac-00000042).

For **additively manufactured 316L stainless steel**, Simonovski et al. (2025) used SPT creep testing at 650°C and found good correlation between SPT and uniaxial creep for time-to-rupture, but identified that LPBF 316L exhibits multiple minima in deflection-rate curves—unlike the single minimum in forged 316L—attributed to possible micro-cracking, which challenges the EN 10371 interpretation procedure (pqac-00000039).

Cannon et al. (2026) demonstrated SPT repeatability on cold-drawn mild steels, using sub-size ASTM E8 dog-bone specimens (8 mm outer diameter, 4 mm reduced diameter, 16 mm gauge length) as reference. They found EN8 had YS = 289 MPa, UTS = 574 MPa, while EN3B had YS = 413 MPa, UTS = 719 MPa (pqac-00000043).

### Size Effects

The thickness-to-grain-size ratio (t/d) is critical for SPT validity: ratios below 25 produce unrepresentative results due to limited geometrically necessary dislocations and low-strain substructural effects. Tested steels had t/d ratios of 45–74, considered representative (pqac-00000043). Decreasing SPT disk thickness from 0.5 to 0.2 mm increased measured strength in Incoloy alloy, attributed to grain-size and dislocation-confinement effects (pqac-00000036). A heterogeneous spatial distribution of strain emphasizes the critical requirement for metallographically homogeneous samples (pqac-00000037).

### Sub-Size ASTM E8 Specimens for AM

Sub-size ASTM E8/E8M tensile specimens (e.g., 4 mm reduced diameter, 16 mm gauge length) are routinely used for AM metals, as evidenced by Kumar et al. (2026) testing AA6061 from additive friction stir deposition and Tello et al. (2026) testing ER308L WAAM stainless steel. These are important because AM build volumes often cannot accommodate full-size specimens, and sub-size specimens enable localized property mapping across a build.

## 4. Automated, Robot-Compatible, and SDL-Integrated Mechanical Testing

### LLNL APEX Platform

The most advanced documented self-driving laboratory for metallurgy is **APEX (Autonomous Alloy Prediction and EXperimentation)** at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, developed with Cornell University. APEX combines robotic handling, directed-energy-deposition (DED) additive manufacturing, automated grinding and polishing, optical microscopy, diamond indentation for hardness, and compression testing. The system can process up to **48 samples per day** with data collected throughout fabrication, preparation, and testing, fed into a Materials Acceleration Platform (MAP) where machine-learning tools guide subsequent compositions (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000054). A vibration sensor on the grinding machine converts the operator's tactile judgment into numerical process data. APEX is initially being trained on stainless-steel alloys and is planned to become extensible by 2027 (pqac-00000046).

### Autonomous AM Laboratory Concepts

Collins and Ales (2026) describe an AM-enabled autonomous laboratory concept integrating agentic AI with Model Context Protocol servers, in-process sensors (cameras, eddy-current sensors, laser-induced phased arrays), and experimental cells for manufacturing, machining, and testing. For mechanical screening, they specifically advocate **hardness indentation and strain-hardening rate as accelerated surrogates for ultimate tensile strength**, avoiding the time cost of full tensile testing (pqac-00000055). Mallia and Caputo (2026) proposed a three-axis taxonomy (Material System State, Hardware Autonomy Level, Software Autonomy Level) for classifying SDLs; bulk metallurgy platforms like APEX are classified as MSS-3/HAL-2/SAL-2 (pqac-00000047).

### Robot-Assisted Experimental Mechanics

Strohmann et al. (2023) demonstrated the closest approach to self-driving mechanical testing, combining a servo-hydraulic fatigue test rig (sinusoidal cycling at 20 Hz, 4.5–15 kN) with a **KUKA LBR iiwa collaborative robot** carrying a Zeiss STEMI 206C optical microscope for high-resolution DIC. The cobot autonomously positions the microscope at crack-tip regions identified by convolutional neural networks (ParallelNets for crack-tip detection, UNetPath for crack-path detection) operating on global GOM Aramis 12M DIC data. The hardware is fully automated for uniaxial testing and has been adapted for biaxial rigs. CrackPy, an open-source Python library, manages the entire workflow (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065).

### High-Throughput Nanoindentation Mapping

Chawla et al. (2026) proposed **random combinatorial libraries** where heterogeneous metallic machining particulates are embedded in conductive epoxy, creating a specimen with hundreds to thousands of discrete compositions in one mount. These are mapped by SEM-EDS (15 kV, 6.4 nA, 20–30 minute acquisitions) and characterized by automated nanoindentation using a KLA iMicro system at 200 nm target depth and 0.2 strain rate. Each indent takes approximately **5 seconds**, with a 5×5 grid requiring ~1280 seconds including positioning (~45 s/indent). Bayesian optimization with Gaussian-process surrogates guides site selection, and the approach is expected to provide **orders-of-magnitude throughput improvement** over sequential library approaches (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). High-throughput nanoindentation on diffusion multiples and sputtered combinatorial libraries has also been demonstrated for alloy screening (pqac-00000032).

## 5. Accuracy Pitfalls of Small / DIY Load Frames

The following table quantifies the major accuracy pitfalls documented in recent literature:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### Key Findings

**Crosshead displacement vs. extensometry.** The single most important accuracy lesson is that crosshead displacement cannot reliably measure strain for modulus determination. The MT-02 open-source UTM underestimated Young's modulus by 48% compared to a commercial machine with video extensometry, because crosshead displacement includes deformation of the load train, grips, and fixtures (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). Meyer et al. (2023) demonstrated that a compliance correction ΔL = ΔX − C_total × P, combined with an effective gauge-length correction, can bring crosshead-derived strain into agreement with extensometer strain within the linear elastic region (up to ~0.5% strain for aluminum and ~1% for PA6), but the correction breaks down at larger strains (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000024). The machine compliance measured by Meyer et al. was 2.5 µm/N using a stiff steel reference specimen (pqac-00000020).

**In-situ stage compliance.** The Deben MT2000EH in-situ rig showed approximately 0.8 µm/N compliance when using dowel-pin specimen fixturing, with the initial bedding-in displacement masking the elastic response. Independent image tracking confirmed that during approximately the first 100 seconds, rig displacement increased while specimen elongation remained negligible (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000048). Clamped grips (as on an Instron) showed a much more rapid initial force rise (pqac-00000019).

**Alignment effects.** A 2° specimen misalignment in the Deben rig changed the fracture mode from tensile to shear, even though the UTS changed only marginally (46.8 to 46.6 MPa). This demonstrates that UTS agreement alone cannot validate alignment quality (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000050). ASTM E1012 classifies alignment quality by the ratio of bending strain to axial strain; for metals testing per ASTM E8/ISO 6892-1, maximum permissible bending strain is typically 5% of the axial strain.

**Dimensional uncertainty.** For small AM specimens, diameter variation of up to 70 µm led to an estimated 14% uncertainty in calculated stress (pqac-00000018). This becomes increasingly problematic as specimens miniaturize.

**Practical recommendations for DIY frames in an SDL context:** (1) Always include independent extensometry or DIC—a camera-based system or clip-on extensometer is essential; (2) Characterize and subtract load-train compliance using a stiff reference specimen; (3) Use clamped rather than pinned grips; (4) Measure every specimen's cross-section individually; (5) Verify alignment under preload; (6) Include a warm-up period and tare procedure to address load-cell drift; (7) Consider nanoindentation hardness as a high-throughput surrogate for tensile properties in early screening, with full tensile testing reserved for promising candidates.

## Summary and Recommendations for SDL Integration

For an autonomous self-driving laboratory performing high-throughput metallurgy and 3D-printed materials research, the following architecture emerges from the literature:

1. **Screening tier:** Use automated nanoindentation mapping on polished cross-sections or combinatorial libraries, as demonstrated by Chawla et al. (2026), to rapidly screen compositions at ~45 seconds/indent with Bayesian optimization guiding site selection (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028).

2. **Intermediate tier:** Use small punch testing (SPT per EN 10371) with 8 mm × 0.5 mm disc specimens to estimate yield and tensile strength from minimal material, particularly valuable for AM builds where material is limited (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

3. **Validation tier:** Use sub-size ASTM E8 tensile specimens with a properly instrumented load frame (>5 kN capacity, video extensometer or DIC, clamped grips) for quantitative stress-strain characterization of selected compositions.

4. **Automation:** The APEX platform (Conn & Baker, 2025) demonstrates that closed-loop DED → grinding → characterization workflows achieving 48 samples/day are feasible (pqac-00000044). Robot-assisted DIC positioning with cobots (Strohmann et al., 2023) shows how mechanical testing can be integrated with autonomous data collection (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064).

5. **Open-source hardware:** Current open-source UTMs (MT-02 at ~3.5 kN, DIY-EMTT at ~98 N) are not yet adequate for metals testing without significant upgrades—particularly the addition of independent extensometry and higher-capacity load cells. The 48% modulus error from crosshead displacement alone underscores that any SDL-integrated tensile frame must include DIC or a video extensometer (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006).

No fully open-source, SDL-ready mechanical testing platform with closed-loop Bayesian optimization driving composition selection through tensile testing has been published as of late 2026. This represents a significant gap and opportunity in the field."}

# Survey of Low-Cost, Open-Source, and DIY Mechanical Test Frames for Autonomous Self-Driving Laboratories in Metallurgy and 3D-Printed Materials Research

## 1. Open-Source / Open-Hardware Tensile and Compression Testing Machines

Several recent open-source mechanical testing designs have been documented, though none yet demonstrate full standards compliance for metals testing (ASTM E8/E8M or ISO 6892-1).

**MT-02 (Demmel, 2024, TU Wien).** This is the most capable recent open-source UTM identified. It uses a 40×80 mm aluminum profile frame, two NEMA 17 stepper motors with 19.203:1 gearboxes driving twin SFU 1605 ball-screw assemblies (500 mm spindles), and a 5 kN load cell. The controller is Arduino-based with a touchscreen display. The rated load capacity is 3.5 kN. Displacement is inferred from motor steps at 5 Hz logging. Testing is displacement-controlled at speeds such as 1 mm/min, with 30–40 N preload. Crucially, validation against a ZwickRoell RetroLine with video extensometer showed that tensile strength agreed within ~1%, but the crosshead-derived strain differed by approximately a factor of two, causing a **48% underestimate of Young's modulus** (demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 1-6, demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 64-68). The design is open-source using FreeCAD, KiCad, PrusaSlicer, and Arduino IDE, though the total BOM cost was not explicitly stated (demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 25-30). It references DIN 50125 and ISO 527-1 specimen geometries but does not claim ASTM E8 or D638 compliance (demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 13-17).

**DIY-EMTT (Wiranata et al., 2024, HardwareX).** This modular design targets stretchable/soft materials. It integrates a NEMA 23 stepper motor with TB6560 driver on a 500 mm aluminum linear stage, a 10 kg (≈98 N) load cell with HX711 amplifier, a VL53L0X time-of-flight displacement sensor, and a built-in resistance meter for simultaneous electromechanical testing. Four Arduino Nano boards coordinate with a LabVIEW GUI. The stated BOM cost is **US$173.28**, and designs are released under CC BY-SA 4.0 via a Mendeley Data repository. GUI speeds of 500, 200, and 100 mm/min are associated with JIS K 6251 / ASTM D412 standards for elastomers, but ASTM E8 or D638 compliance is not demonstrated (wiranata2024economicallyviableelectromechanical pages 9-11, wiranata2024economicallyviableelectromechanical pages 3-6, wiranata2024economicallyviableelectromechanical pages 1-3).

## 2. In-Situ / Miniature Tensile Stages

**Commercial in-situ stages.** The best-documented commercial stage in recent literature is the **Deben MT2000EH**, a single-leadscrew miniature tensile/compression stage designed for use inside SEM, optical microscopy, AFM, and XRD systems. NPL found its system compliance to be approximately 0.8 µm/N when using dowel-pin fixturing, reducing to <0.001 µm/N with a very stiff specimen (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 13-17, koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 8-13). The Deben was validated against an Instron 5969: peak loads differed by only ±0.8 N for lattice specimens with five and two unit cells, and by ~4.6 ± 2.2 N for single-cell specimens (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 23-28). A separate assessment of a 5 kN single-leadscrew rig (likely also Deben/NewTec family) found that recorded versus image-tracked displacement showed only R² = 0.79, representing more than 20% inconsistency (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 31-35).

Other major commercial in-situ stage manufacturers include **Deben Microtest** (200 N to 10 kN range; typical price ~$15,000–50,000+), **Kammrath & Weiss** (tensile/compression/bending stages for SEM, 1–10 kN, with symmetric dual-actuator designs that keep the gauge section stationary), **Psylotech** (µTS micro-tensile stages, 100 N–5 kN), **MTI Instruments SEMtester** (various load ranges), **Linkam TST350** (temperature-controlled tensile stage for optical/X-ray, ≤2.2 kN), **Alemnis** (micro/nano-mechanical testing in SEM), and **Bruker/Hysitron PI series** (nanomechanical testing). Price bands typically range from ~$15,000 for basic stages to >$100,000 for fully featured systems with environmental control.

**Symmetric/dual-opposed actuator designs** that keep the gauge section stationary during testing are commercially available from Kammrath & Weiss and some Psylotech models. This is particularly important for in-situ DIC or SEM observation, where the region of interest should remain in the field of view throughout deformation.

**Open-source in-situ stages** specifically designed for SEM or microscopy use were not identified in the 2024–2026 literature search, representing a significant gap. The Camelot system (Trozzi et al., 2025) could potentially be adapted for microscopy-compatible use given its compact form factor and camera-based tracking.

## 3. Miniature and Sub-Size Specimens for AM Metals

### Small Punch Test (SPT)

The small punch test per **EN 10371:2021** uses a miniature disc specimen of **8 ± 0.1 mm diameter and 0.5 ± 0.005 mm thickness**, clamped between dies and loaded by a hemispherical punch (1.25 mm radius) at 0.5 mm/min until rupture (simonovski2025prequalificationofadditively pages 1-2, keshavlal2023investigationofmechanical pages 11-16, keshavlal2023investigationofmechanical pages 8-11). Yield strength is estimated from the elastic-plastic transition force F_e using the empirical correlation σ_YS = β_y × F_e / h₀², where the EN 10371 best-fit constant is β_y = 0.510 for steels with YS between 200–1000 MPa. Ultimate tensile strength is estimated from maximum force F_m and displacement at F_m. Recent work has improved these correlations to achieve R² > 0.95 with errors limited to ±10% (keshavlal2023investigationofmechanical pages 8-11).

For **additively manufactured 316L stainless steel**, Simonovski et al. (2025) used SPT creep testing at 650°C and found good correlation between SPT and uniaxial creep for time-to-rupture, but identified that LPBF 316L exhibits multiple minima in deflection-rate curves—unlike the single minimum in forged 316L—attributed to possible micro-cracking, which challenges the EN 10371 interpretation procedure (simonovski2025prequalificationofadditively pages 1-2).

Cannon et al. (2026) demonstrated SPT repeatability on cold-drawn mild steels, using sub-size ASTM E8 dog-bone specimens (8 mm outer diameter, 4 mm reduced diameter, 16 mm gauge length) as reference. They found EN8 had YS = 289 MPa, UTS = 574 MPa, while EN3B had YS = 413 MPa, UTS = 719 MPa (cannon2026evaluationofthe pages 3-4).

### Size Effects

The thickness-to-grain-size ratio (t/d) is critical for SPT validity: ratios below 25 produce unrepresentative results due to limited geometrically necessary dislocations and low-strain substructural effects. Tested steels had t/d ratios of 45–74, considered representative (cannon2026evaluationofthe pages 3-4). Decreasing SPT disk thickness from 0.5 to 0.2 mm increased measured strength in Incoloy alloy, attributed to grain-size and dislocation-confinement effects (cannon2026evaluationofthe pages 2-3). A heterogeneous spatial distribution of strain emphasizes the critical requirement for metallographically homogeneous samples (cannon2026evaluationofthe pages 1-2).

### Sub-Size ASTM E8 Specimens for AM

Sub-size ASTM E8/E8M tensile specimens (e.g., 4 mm reduced diameter, 16 mm gauge length) are routinely used for AM metals, as evidenced by Kumar et al. (2026) testing AA6061 from additive friction stir deposition and Tello et al. (2026) testing ER308L WAAM stainless steel. These are important because AM build volumes often cannot accommodate full-size specimens, and sub-size specimens enable localized property mapping across a build.

## 4. Automated, Robot-Compatible, and SDL-Integrated Mechanical Testing

### LLNL APEX Platform

The most advanced documented self-driving laboratory for metallurgy is **APEX (Autonomous Alloy Prediction and EXperimentation)** at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, developed with Cornell University. APEX combines robotic handling, directed-energy-deposition (DED) additive manufacturing, automated grinding and polishing, optical microscopy, diamond indentation for hardness, and compression testing. The system can process up to **48 samples per day** with data collected throughout fabrication, preparation, and testing, fed into a Materials Acceleration Platform (MAP) where machine-learning tools guide subsequent compositions (conn2025selfdrivinglabto pages 1-8). A vibration sensor on the grinding machine converts the operator's tactile judgment into numerical process data. APEX is initially being trained on stainless-steel alloys and is planned to become extensible by 2027 (conn2025selfdrivinglabto pages 8-8).

### Autonomous AM Laboratory Concepts

Collins and Ales (2026) describe an AM-enabled autonomous laboratory concept integrating agentic AI with Model Context Protocol servers, in-process sensors (cameras, eddy-current sensors, laser-induced phased arrays), and experimental cells for manufacturing, machining, and testing. For mechanical screening, they specifically advocate **hardness indentation and strain-hardening rate as accelerated surrogates for ultimate tensile strength**, avoiding the time cost of full tensile testing (collins2026additivemanufacturingenabled pages 18-20). Mallia and Caputo (2026) proposed a three-axis taxonomy (Material System State, Hardware Autonomy Level, Software Autonomy Level) for classifying SDLs; bulk metallurgy platforms like APEX are classified as MSS-3/HAL-2/SAL-2 (mallia2026aiguidedselfdrivinglaboratories pages 6-12).

### Robot-Assisted Experimental Mechanics

Strohmann et al. (2023) demonstrated the closest approach to self-driving mechanical testing, combining a servo-hydraulic fatigue test rig (sinusoidal cycling at 20 Hz, 4.5–15 kN) with a **KUKA LBR iiwa collaborative robot** carrying a Zeiss STEMI 206C optical microscope for high-resolution DIC. The cobot autonomously positions the microscope at crack-tip regions identified by convolutional neural networks (ParallelNets for crack-tip detection, UNetPath for crack-path detection) operating on global GOM Aramis 12M DIC data. The hardware is fully automated for uniaxial testing and has been adapted for biaxial rigs. CrackPy, an open-source Python library, manages the entire workflow (strohmann2023towardsselfdrivinglabs pages 1-4, strohmann2023towardsselfdrivinglabs pages 4-6, strohmann2023towardsselfdrivinglabs pages 9-11, strohmann2023towardsselfdrivinglabs pages 6-9).

### High-Throughput Nanoindentation Mapping

Chawla et al. (2026) proposed **random combinatorial libraries** where heterogeneous metallic machining particulates are embedded in conductive epoxy, creating a specimen with hundreds to thousands of discrete compositions in one mount. These are mapped by SEM-EDS (15 kV, 6.4 nA, 20–30 minute acquisitions) and characterized by automated nanoindentation using a KLA iMicro system at 200 nm target depth and 0.2 strain rate. Each indent takes approximately **5 seconds**, with a 5×5 grid requiring ~1280 seconds including positioning (~45 s/indent). Bayesian optimization with Gaussian-process surrogates guides site selection, and the approach is expected to provide **orders-of-magnitude throughput improvement** over sequential library approaches (chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 6-9, chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 13-16, chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 16-18, chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 9-13). High-throughput nanoindentation on diffusion multiples and sputtered combinatorial libraries has also been demonstrated for alloy screening (mooraj2023areviewon pages 28-30).

## 5. Accuracy Pitfalls of Small / DIY Load Frames

The following table quantifies the major accuracy pitfalls documented in recent literature:

| Error source | Typical magnitude / consequence | How detected or quantified | Mitigation | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Crosshead-derived modulus error | MT-02 underestimated Young’s modulus by **48%** relative to a commercial frame using video extensometry; crosshead-derived strain differed by approximately a factor of two. | Parallel tests on the MT-02 and a ZwickRoell frame; comparison of motor-step-derived crosshead strain with optically measured gauge strain. | Use a video extensometer or DIC on the gauge section. If crosshead data must be used, characterize and subtract load-train compliance. | Demmel 2024 (demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 1-6, demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 64-68, demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 50-54) |
| Machine and fixture compliance | Reported values include **2.5 µm/N** for one machine/fixture, approximately **0.8 µm/N** for the Deben pin-mounted configuration, and **<0.001 µm/N** when the Deben system was checked using a very stiff specimen. | Load a reference specimen much stiffer than the intended specimen and fit the force-dependent extra displacement. Compare stage displacement with direct image tracking. | Determine configuration-specific total compliance, `C_total`, and calculate specimen extension as `ΔL = ΔX − C_total·P`. Recalibrate after changing grips, load cell, fixtures, or specimen geometry. | Meyer 2023; Koko et al. 2024 (meyer2023testmethodsfor pages 10-11, koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 13-17) |
| Specimen misalignment | A **2°** angular error changed the observed failure from predominantly tensile to shear, although UTS changed only marginally from **46.8 to 46.6 MPa**. Thus, agreement in UTS alone can conceal a seriously non-uniaxial test. | Compare fracture mode and full-field strain/stress distribution for aligned and deliberately misaligned specimens. Use opposing strain gauges or DIC fields to quantify bending. | Use precision-machined, self-aligning fixtures; control grip parallelism and specimen centering; verify alignment under preload and qualify the train using ASTM E1012 procedures. | Koko et al. 2024 (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 28-31) |
| Dimensional uncertainty | Diameter variation as large as **70 µm** produced an estimated **14% uncertainty in calculated stress**. The problem becomes more severe as specimen cross-sectional area decreases. | Measure cross-section at multiple positions and propagate area uncertainty through `σ = F/A`; inspect AM specimens for taper, porosity, and non-circularity. | Measure every specimen individually with calibrated optical or dimensional metrology; use the local gauge-section area rather than nominal CAD dimensions; retain dimensional uncertainty in reported results. | Koko et al. 2024 (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 17-23) |
| Load-cell zero offset or “phantom force” | Apparent preload/phantom force was approximately **2.1 ± 1.3 N**—material for low-capacity cells and micro-specimens. | Record unloaded and lightly preloaded baselines; repeat zero checks before and after tests and monitor warm-up drift. | Warm up electronics, tare immediately before each test, use a consistent seating/preload protocol, calibrate with traceable masses or standards, and include zero drift in the uncertainty budget. | Koko et al. 2024 (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 17-23, koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 28-31) |
| Stage-displacement inconsistency | In a 5 kN single-leadscrew rig, commanded/recorded displacement versus image-tracked displacement gave **R² = 0.79**, characterized as more than **20% inconsistency**. | Track a fixed feature using calibrated SEM or optical images while commanding known unloaded movements; compare actual and reported displacement over the usable travel. | Add an independent encoder, LVDT, optical scale, or image-based displacement channel; calibrate across travel, speed, direction, and load rather than relying on lead-screw pitch or step count alone. | Koko et al. 2024, NewTec appendix (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 31-35) |
| Dowel/pin grip seating and compliance | Pin-mounted specimens exhibited an initial **lead-in/bedding-in displacement** that masked the elastic response; independently tracked specimen elongation remained small while rig displacement increased. Clamped Instron grips showed a much faster initial force rise. | Compare machine displacement with direct optical gauge displacement and compare pin-mounted versus fully clamped fixtures. Examine loading–unloading cycles for seating, slip, and hysteresis. | Prefer clamped or positively located grips where feasible; preload and reseat consistently; exclude seating data; quantify fixture-specific compliance; monitor gauge marks for slip. | Koko et al. 2024 (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 17-23, koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 23-28) |
| Limited validity of linear compliance correction | The demonstrated correction agreed with extensometry only in the linear region—approximately to **0.5% strain for AlMg3** and **1% for PA6**. A constant-compliance elastic correction is not valid through nonlinear deformation. | Compare corrected crosshead strain with extensometer strain over the complete stress–strain curve and identify where their slopes diverge. | Use `ΔL = ΔX − C_total·P` only where load-train response is linear; use direct extensometry/DIC or a validated nonlinear load-train model beyond the elastic regime. | Meyer et al. 2023 (meyer2023testmethodsfor pages 6-8, meyer2023testmethodsfor pages 5-6) |


*Table: Quantified error sources reported for DIY and miniature mechanical test frames, together with practical detection and mitigation methods. The table highlights why direct gauge-section extensometry and configuration-specific compliance calibration are essential.*

### Key Findings

**Crosshead displacement vs. extensometry.** The single most important accuracy lesson is that crosshead displacement cannot reliably measure strain for modulus determination. The MT-02 open-source UTM underestimated Young's modulus by 48% compared to a commercial machine with video extensometry, because crosshead displacement includes deformation of the load train, grips, and fixtures (demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 1-6, demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 64-68). Meyer et al. (2023) demonstrated that a compliance correction ΔL = ΔX − C_total × P, combined with an effective gauge-length correction, can bring crosshead-derived strain into agreement with extensometer strain within the linear elastic region (up to ~0.5% strain for aluminum and ~1% for PA6), but the correction breaks down at larger strains (meyer2023testmethodsfor pages 6-8, meyer2023testmethodsfor pages 5-6). The machine compliance measured by Meyer et al. was 2.5 µm/N using a stiff steel reference specimen (meyer2023testmethodsfor pages 10-11).

**In-situ stage compliance.** The Deben MT2000EH in-situ rig showed approximately 0.8 µm/N compliance when using dowel-pin specimen fixturing, with the initial bedding-in displacement masking the elastic response. Independent image tracking confirmed that during approximately the first 100 seconds, rig displacement increased while specimen elongation remained negligible (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 23-28, koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 13-17). Clamped grips (as on an Instron) showed a much more rapid initial force rise (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 23-28).

**Alignment effects.** A 2° specimen misalignment in the Deben rig changed the fracture mode from tensile to shear, even though the UTS changed only marginally (46.8 to 46.6 MPa). This demonstrates that UTS agreement alone cannot validate alignment quality (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 28-31). ASTM E1012 classifies alignment quality by the ratio of bending strain to axial strain; for metals testing per ASTM E8/ISO 6892-1, maximum permissible bending strain is typically 5% of the axial strain.

**Dimensional uncertainty.** For small AM specimens, diameter variation of up to 70 µm led to an estimated 14% uncertainty in calculated stress (koko2024uncertaintiesofit pages 17-23). This becomes increasingly problematic as specimens miniaturize.

**Practical recommendations for DIY frames in an SDL context:** (1) Always include independent extensometry or DIC—a camera-based system or clip-on extensometer is essential; (2) Characterize and subtract load-train compliance using a stiff reference specimen; (3) Use clamped rather than pinned grips; (4) Measure every specimen's cross-section individually; (5) Verify alignment under preload; (6) Include a warm-up period and tare procedure to address load-cell drift; (7) Consider nanoindentation hardness as a high-throughput surrogate for tensile properties in early screening, with full tensile testing reserved for promising candidates.

## Summary and Recommendations for SDL Integration

For an autonomous self-driving laboratory performing high-throughput metallurgy and 3D-printed materials research, the following architecture emerges from the literature:

1. **Screening tier:** Use automated nanoindentation mapping on polished cross-sections or combinatorial libraries, as demonstrated by Chawla et al. (2026), to rapidly screen compositions at ~45 seconds/indent with Bayesian optimization guiding site selection (chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 6-9, chawla2026randomcombinatoriallibraries pages 16-18).

2. **Intermediate tier:** Use small punch testing (SPT per EN 10371) with 8 mm × 0.5 mm disc specimens to estimate yield and tensile strength from minimal material, particularly valuable for AM builds where material is limited (simonovski2025prequalificationofadditively pages 1-2, keshavlal2023investigationofmechanical pages 11-16).

3. **Validation tier:** Use sub-size ASTM E8 tensile specimens with a properly instrumented load frame (>5 kN capacity, video extensometer or DIC, clamped grips) for quantitative stress-strain characterization of selected compositions.

4. **Automation:** The APEX platform (Conn & Baker, 2025) demonstrates that closed-loop DED → grinding → characterization workflows achieving 48 samples/day are feasible (conn2025selfdrivinglabto pages 1-8). Robot-assisted DIC positioning with cobots (Strohmann et al., 2023) shows how mechanical testing can be integrated with autonomous data collection (strohmann2023towardsselfdrivinglabs pages 1-4, strohmann2023towardsselfdrivinglabs pages 9-11).

5. **Open-source hardware:** Current open-source UTMs (MT-02 at ~3.5 kN, DIY-EMTT at ~98 N) are not yet adequate for metals testing without significant upgrades—particularly the addition of independent extensometry and higher-capacity load cells. The 48% modulus error from crosshead displacement alone underscores that any SDL-integrated tensile frame must include DIC or a video extensometer (demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 1-6, demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 64-68).

No fully open-source, SDL-ready mechanical testing platform with closed-loop Bayesian optimization driving composition selection through tensile testing has been published as of late 2026. This represents a significant gap and opportunity in the field.

# Survey of Low-Cost, Open-Source, and DIY Mechanical Test Frames for Autonomous Self-Driving Laboratories in Metallurgy and 3D-Printed Materials Research

## 1. Open-Source / Open-Hardware Tensile and Compression Testing Machines

Several recent open-source mechanical testing designs have been documented, though none yet demonstrate full standards compliance for metals testing (ASTM E8/E8M or ISO 6892-1).

**MT-02 (Demmel, 2024, TU Wien).** This is the most capable recent open-source UTM identified. It uses a 40×80 mm aluminum profile frame, two NEMA 17 stepper motors with 19.203:1 gearboxes driving twin SFU 1605 ball-screw assemblies (500 mm spindles), and a 5 kN load cell. The controller is Arduino-based with a touchscreen display. The rated load capacity is 3.5 kN. Displacement is inferred from motor steps at 5 Hz logging. Testing is displacement-controlled at speeds such as 1 mm/min, with 30–40 N preload. Crucially, validation against a ZwickRoell RetroLine with video extensometer showed that tensile strength agreed within ~1%, but the crosshead-derived strain differed by approximately a factor of two, causing a **48% underestimate of Young's modulus** (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). The design is open-source using FreeCAD, KiCad, PrusaSlicer, and Arduino IDE, though the total BOM cost was not explicitly stated (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008). It references DIN 50125 and ISO 527-1 specimen geometries but does not claim ASTM E8 or D638 compliance (pqac-00000000).

**DIY-EMTT (Wiranata et al., 2024, HardwareX).** This modular design targets stretchable/soft materials. It integrates a NEMA 23 stepper motor with TB6560 driver on a 500 mm aluminum linear stage, a 10 kg (≈98 N) load cell with HX711 amplifier, a VL53L0X time-of-flight displacement sensor, and a built-in resistance meter for simultaneous electromechanical testing. Four Arduino Nano boards coordinate with a LabVIEW GUI. The stated BOM cost is **US$173.28**, and designs are released under CC BY-SA 4.0 via a Mendeley Data repository. GUI speeds of 500, 200, and 100 mm/min are associated with JIS K 6251 / ASTM D412 standards for elastomers, but ASTM E8 or D638 compliance is not demonstrated (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012).

**Camelot Micro-Extensometer (Trozzi et al., 2025, BMC Biology).** This is a low-cost system designed for plant biomechanics rather than engineering materials, but its architecture is instructive. It uses interchangeable parallel-beam load sensors (from ~10 g to several kg capacity, ≈£10 each; the 10 g sensor provides ~10 µN resolution), a stepper motor with a 1 mm pitch screw producing 5 µm steps, and camera-based optical tracking providing ~5 µm displacement resolution. The actuator costs approximately £50. The open-source MorphoRobotX software runs on Linux (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007).

**Arduino UTM (Geasa, 2021).** A minimal design using a steel frame, NEMA 23 stepper motor (19 kg·cm torque, 1.8° step angle), TB6600 driver, lead-screw actuator, and a load cell with Arduino logging. Total cost was below 1,000 Egyptian pounds (approximately US$20–30 at the time). Displacement is controlled through motor steps with no independent sensor (pqac-00000014).

An additional notable design is the **open-source flexible material tensile testing apparatus by Woods et al. (2024)** published in the journal *Hardware* (DOI: 10.3390/hardware2010002), though full details could not be retrieved in this search.
