## 2. In-Situ / Miniature Tensile Stages

**Commercial in-situ stages.** The best-documented commercial stage in recent literature is the **Deben MT2000EH**, a single-leadscrew miniature tensile/compression stage designed for use inside SEM, optical microscopy, AFM, and XRD systems. As characterized by the UK National Physical Laboratory (NPL), it features a 2 kN load cell with ±0.1% full-scale accuracy, supports tensile, compression, and horizontal bending modes, and uses stainless-steel slide bearings with specimens mounted on 3.25 mm tool-steel rods. NPL found its system compliance to be approximately 0.8 µm/N when using dowel-pin fixturing, reducing to <0.001 µm/N with a very stiff specimen (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000023). The Deben was validated against an Instron 5969: peak loads differed by only ±0.8 N for lattice specimens with five and two unit cells, and by ~4.6 ± 2.2 N for single-cell specimens (pqac-00000051). A separate assessment of a 5 kN single-leadscrew rig (likely also Deben/NewTec family) found that recorded versus image-tracked displacement showed only R² = 0.79, representing more than 20% inconsistency (pqac-00000053).

Other major commercial in-situ stage manufacturers include **Deben Microtest** (200 N to 10 kN range; typical price ~$15,000–50,000+), **Kammrath & Weiss** (tensile/compression/bending stages for SEM, 1–10 kN, with symmetric dual-actuator designs that keep the gauge section stationary), **Psylotech** (µTS micro-tensile stages, 100 N–5 kN), **MTI Instruments SEMtester** (various load ranges), **Linkam TST350** (temperature-controlled tensile stage for optical/X-ray, ≤2.2 kN), **Alemnis** (micro/nano-mechanical testing in SEM), and **Bruker/Hysitron PI series** (nanomechanical testing). Price bands typically range from ~$15,000 for basic stages to >$100,000 for fully featured systems with environmental control.

**Symmetric/dual-opposed actuator designs** that keep the gauge section stationary during testing are commercially available from Kammrath & Weiss and some Psylotech models. This is particularly important for in-situ DIC or SEM observation, where the region of interest should remain in the field of view throughout deformation.

**Open-source in-situ stages** specifically designed for SEM or microscopy use were not identified in the 2024–2026 literature search, representing a significant gap. The Camelot system (Trozzi et al., 2025) could potentially be adapted for microscopy-compatible use given its compact form factor and camera-based tracking.

## 3. Miniature and Sub-Size Specimens for AM Metals

### Small Punch Test (SPT)

The small punch test per **EN 10371:2021** uses a miniature disc specimen of **8 ± 0.1 mm diameter and 0.5 ± 0.005 mm thickness**, clamped between dies and loaded by a hemispherical punch (1.25 mm radius) at 0.5 mm/min until rupture (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042). Yield strength is estimated from the elastic-plastic transition force F_e using the empirical correlation σ_YS = β_y × F_e / h₀², where the EN 10371 best-fit constant is β_y = 0.510 for steels with YS between 200–1000 MPa. Ultimate tensile strength is estimated from maximum force F_m and displacement at F_m. Recent work has improved these correlations to achieve R² > 0.95 with errors limited to ±10% (pqac-00000042).

For **additively manufactured 316L stainless steel**, Simonovski et al. (2025) used SPT creep testing at 650°C and found good correlation between SPT and uniaxial creep for time-to-rupture, but identified that LPBF 316L exhibits multiple minima in deflection-rate curves—unlike the single minimum in forged 316L—attributed to possible micro-cracking, which challenges the EN 10371 interpretation procedure (pqac-00000039).

Cannon et al. (2026) demonstrated SPT repeatability on cold-drawn mild steels, using sub-size ASTM E8 dog-bone specimens (8 mm outer diameter, 4 mm reduced diameter, 16 mm gauge length) as reference. They found EN8 had YS = 289 MPa, UTS = 574 MPa, while EN3B had YS = 413 MPa, UTS = 719 MPa (pqac-00000043).

### Size Effects

The thickness-to-grain-size ratio (t/d) is critical for SPT validity: ratios below 25 produce unrepresentative results due to limited geometrically necessary dislocations and low-strain substructural effects. Tested steels had t/d ratios of 45–74, considered representative (pqac-00000043). Decreasing SPT disk thickness from 0.5 to 0.2 mm increased measured strength in Incoloy alloy, attributed to grain-size and dislocation-confinement effects (pqac-00000036). A heterogeneous spatial distribution of strain emphasizes the critical requirement for metallographically homogeneous samples (pqac-00000037).

### Sub-Size ASTM E8 Specimens for AM

Sub-size ASTM E8/E8M tensile specimens (e.g., 4 mm reduced diameter, 16 mm gauge length) are routinely used for AM metals, as evidenced by Kumar et al. (2026) testing AA6061 from additive friction stir deposition and Tello et al. (2026) testing ER308L WAAM stainless steel. These are important because AM build volumes often cannot accommodate full-size specimens, and sub-size specimens enable localized property mapping across a build.

## 4. Automated, Robot-Compatible, and SDL-Integrated Mechanical Testing

### LLNL APEX Platform

The most advanced documented self-driving laboratory for metallurgy is **APEX (Autonomous Alloy Prediction and EXperimentation)** at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, developed with Cornell University. APEX combines robotic handling, directed-energy-deposition (DED) additive manufacturing, automated grinding and polishing, optical microscopy, diamond indentation for hardness, and compression testing. The system can process up to **48 samples per day** with data collected throughout fabrication, preparation, and testing, fed into a Materials Acceleration Platform (MAP) where machine-learning tools guide subsequent compositions (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000054). A vibration sensor on the grinding machine converts the operator's tactile judgment into numerical process data. APEX is initially being trained on stainless-steel alloys and is planned to become extensible by 2027 (pqac-00000046).

### Autonomous AM Laboratory Concepts

Collins and Ales (2026) describe an AM-enabled autonomous laboratory concept integrating agentic AI with Model Context Protocol servers, in-process sensors (cameras, eddy-current sensors, laser-induced phased arrays), and experimental cells for manufacturing, machining, and testing. For mechanical screening, they specifically advocate **hardness indentation and strain-hardening rate as accelerated surrogates for ultimate tensile strength**, avoiding the time cost of full tensile testing (pqac-00000055). Mallia and Caputo (2026) proposed a three-axis taxonomy (Material System State, Hardware Autonomy Level, Software Autonomy Level) for classifying SDLs; bulk metallurgy platforms like APEX are classified as MSS-3/HAL-2/SAL-2 (pqac-00000047).

### Robot-Assisted Experimental Mechanics

Strohmann et al. (2023) demonstrated the closest approach to self-driving mechanical testing, combining a servo-hydraulic fatigue test rig (sinusoidal cycling at 20 Hz, 4.5–15 kN) with a **KUKA LBR iiwa collaborative robot** carrying a Zeiss STEMI 206C optical microscope for high-resolution DIC. The cobot autonomously positions the microscope at crack-tip regions identified by convolutional neural networks (ParallelNets for crack-tip detection, UNetPath for crack-path detection) operating on global GOM Aramis 12M DIC data. The hardware is fully automated for uniaxial testing and has been adapted for biaxial rigs. CrackPy, an open-source Python library, manages the entire workflow (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000065).

### High-Throughput Nanoindentation Mapping

Chawla et al. (2026) proposed **random combinatorial libraries** where heterogeneous metallic machining particulates are embedded in conductive epoxy, creating a specimen with hundreds to thousands of discrete compositions in one mount. These are mapped by SEM-EDS (15 kV, 6.4 nA, 20–30 minute acquisitions) and characterized by automated nanoindentation using a KLA iMicro system at 200 nm target depth and 0.2 strain rate. Each indent takes approximately **5 seconds**, with a 5×5 grid requiring ~1280 seconds including positioning (~45 s/indent). Bayesian optimization with Gaussian-process surrogates guides site selection, and the approach is expected to provide **orders-of-magnitude throughput improvement** over sequential library approaches (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). High-throughput nanoindentation on diffusion multiples and sputtered combinatorial libraries has also been demonstrated for alloy screening (pqac-00000032).

## 5. Accuracy Pitfalls of Small / DIY Load Frames

The following table quantifies the major accuracy pitfalls documented in recent literature:

| Error source | Typical magnitude / consequence | How detected or quantified | Mitigation | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Crosshead-derived modulus error | MT-02 underestimated Young’s modulus by **48%** relative to a commercial frame using video extensometry; crosshead-derived strain differed by approximately a factor of two. | Parallel tests on the MT-02 and a ZwickRoell frame; comparison of motor-step-derived crosshead strain with optically measured gauge strain. | Use a video extensometer or DIC on the gauge section. If crosshead data must be used, characterize and subtract load-train compliance. | Demmel 2024 (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000013) |
| Machine and fixture compliance | Reported values include **2.5 µm/N** for one machine/fixture, approximately **0.8 µm/N** for the Deben pin-mounted configuration, and **<0.001 µm/N** when the Deben system was checked using a very stiff specimen. | Load a reference specimen much stiffer than the intended specimen and fit the force-dependent extra displacement. Compare stage displacement with direct image tracking. | Determine configuration-specific total compliance, `C_total`, and calculate specimen extension as `ΔL = ΔX − C_total·P`. Recalibrate after changing grips, load cell, fixtures, or specimen geometry. | Meyer 2023; Koko et al. 2024 (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000048) |
| Specimen misalignment | A **2°** angular error changed the observed failure from predominantly tensile to shear, although UTS changed only marginally from **46.8 to 46.6 MPa**. Thus, agreement in UTS alone can conceal a seriously non-uniaxial test. | Compare fracture mode and full-field strain/stress distribution for aligned and deliberately misaligned specimens. Use opposing strain gauges or DIC fields to quantify bending. | Use precision-machined, self-aligning fixtures; control grip parallelism and specimen centering; verify alignment under preload and qualify the train using ASTM E1012 procedures. | Koko et al. 2024 (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000050) |
| Dimensional uncertainty | Diameter variation as large as **70 µm** produced an estimated **14% uncertainty in calculated stress**. The problem becomes more severe as specimen cross-sectional area decreases. | Measure cross-section at multiple positions and propagate area uncertainty through `σ = F/A`; inspect AM specimens for taper, porosity, and non-circularity. | Measure every specimen individually with calibrated optical or dimensional metrology; use the local gauge-section area rather than nominal CAD dimensions; retain dimensional uncertainty in reported results. | Koko et al. 2024 (pqac-00000018) |
| Load-cell zero offset or “phantom force” | Apparent preload/phantom force was approximately **2.1 ± 1.3 N**—material for low-capacity cells and micro-specimens. | Record unloaded and lightly preloaded baselines; repeat zero checks before and after tests and monitor warm-up drift. | Warm up electronics, tare immediately before each test, use a consistent seating/preload protocol, calibrate with traceable masses or standards, and include zero drift in the uncertainty budget. | Koko et al. 2024 (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000050) |
| Stage-displacement inconsistency | In a 5 kN single-leadscrew rig, commanded/recorded displacement versus image-tracked displacement gave **R² = 0.79**, characterized as more than **20% inconsistency**. | Track a fixed feature using calibrated SEM or optical images while commanding known unloaded movements; compare actual and reported displacement over the usable travel. | Add an independent encoder, LVDT, optical scale, or image-based displacement channel; calibrate across travel, speed, direction, and load rather than relying on lead-screw pitch or step count alone. | Koko et al. 2024, NewTec appendix (pqac-00000053) |
| Dowel/pin grip seating and compliance | Pin-mounted specimens exhibited an initial **lead-in/bedding-in displacement** that masked the elastic response; independently tracked specimen elongation remained small while rig displacement increased. Clamped Instron grips showed a much faster initial force rise. | Compare machine displacement with direct optical gauge displacement and compare pin-mounted versus fully clamped fixtures. Examine loading–unloading cycles for seating, slip, and hysteresis. | Prefer clamped or positively located grips where feasible; preload and reseat consistently; exclude seating data; quantify fixture-specific compliance; monitor gauge marks for slip. | Koko et al. 2024 (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000051) |
| Limited validity of linear compliance correction | The demonstrated correction agreed with extensometry only in the linear region—approximately to **0.5% strain for AlMg3** and **1% for PA6**. A constant-compliance elastic correction is not valid through nonlinear deformation. | Compare corrected crosshead strain with extensometer strain over the complete stress–strain curve and identify where their slopes diverge. | Use `ΔL = ΔX − C_total·P` only where load-train response is linear; use direct extensometry/DIC or a validated nonlinear load-train model beyond the elastic regime. | Meyer et al. 2023 (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000024) |


*Table: Quantified error sources reported for DIY and miniature mechanical test frames, together with practical detection and mitigation methods. The table highlights why direct gauge-section extensometry and configuration-specific compliance calibration are essential.*

### Key Findings

**Crosshead displacement vs. extensometry.** The single most important accuracy lesson is that crosshead displacement cannot reliably measure strain for modulus determination. The MT-02 open-source UTM underestimated Young's modulus by 48% compared to a commercial machine with video extensometry, because crosshead displacement includes deformation of the load train, grips, and fixtures (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006). Meyer et al. (2023) demonstrated that a compliance correction ΔL = ΔX − C_total × P, combined with an effective gauge-length correction, can bring crosshead-derived strain into agreement with extensometer strain within the linear elastic region (up to ~0.5% strain for aluminum and ~1% for PA6), but the correction breaks down at larger strains (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000024). The machine compliance measured by Meyer et al. was 2.5 µm/N using a stiff steel reference specimen (pqac-00000020).

**In-situ stage compliance.** The Deben MT2000EH in-situ rig showed approximately 0.8 µm/N compliance when using dowel-pin specimen fixturing, with the initial bedding-in displacement masking the elastic response. Independent image tracking confirmed that during approximately the first 100 seconds, rig displacement increased while specimen elongation remained negligible (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000048). Clamped grips (as on an Instron) showed a much more rapid initial force rise (pqac-00000019).

**Alignment effects.** A 2° specimen misalignment in the Deben rig changed the fracture mode from tensile to shear, even though the UTS changed only marginally (46.8 to 46.6 MPa). This demonstrates that UTS agreement alone cannot validate alignment quality (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000050). ASTM E1012 classifies alignment quality by the ratio of bending strain to axial strain; for metals testing per ASTM E8/ISO 6892-1, maximum permissible bending strain is typically 5% of the axial strain.

**Dimensional uncertainty.** For small AM specimens, diameter variation of up to 70 µm led to an estimated 14% uncertainty in calculated stress (pqac-00000018). This becomes increasingly problematic as specimens miniaturize.

**Practical recommendations for DIY frames in an SDL context:** (1) Always include independent extensometry or DIC—a camera-based system or clip-on extensometer is essential; (2) Characterize and subtract load-train compliance using a stiff reference specimen; (3) Use clamped rather than pinned grips; (4) Measure every specimen's cross-section individually; (5) Verify alignment under preload; (6) Include a warm-up period and tare procedure to address load-cell drift; (7) Consider nanoindentation hardness as a high-throughput surrogate for tensile properties in early screening, with full tensile testing reserved for promising candidates.

## Summary and Recommendations for SDL Integration

For an autonomous self-driving laboratory performing high-throughput metallurgy and 3D-printed materials research, the following architecture emerges from the literature:

1. **Screening tier:** Use automated nanoindentation mapping on polished cross-sections or combinatorial libraries, as demonstrated by Chawla et al. (2026), to rapidly screen compositions at ~45 seconds/indent with Bayesian optimization guiding site selection (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028).

2. **Intermediate tier:** Use small punch testing (SPT per EN 10371) with 8 mm × 0.5 mm disc specimens to estimate yield and tensile strength from minimal material, particularly valuable for AM builds where material is limited (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040).

3. **Validation tier:** Use sub-size ASTM E8 tensile specimens with a properly instrumented load frame (>5 kN capacity, video extensometer or DIC, clamped grips) for quantitative stress-strain characterization of selected compositions.

4. **Automation:** The APEX platform (Conn & Baker, 2025) demonstrates that closed-loop DED → grinding → characterization workflows achieving 48 samples/day are feasible (pqac-00000044). Robot-assisted DIC positioning with cobots (Strohmann et al., 2023) shows how mechanical testing can be integrated with autonomous data collection (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064).

5. **Open-source hardware:** Current open-source UTMs (MT-02 at ~3.5 kN, DIY-EMTT at ~98 N) are not yet adequate for metals testing without significant upgrades—particularly the addition of independent extensometry and higher-capacity load cells. The 48% modulus error from crosshead displacement alone underscores that any SDL-integrated tensile frame must include DIC or a video extensometer (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006).

No fully open-source, SDL-ready mechanical testing platform with closed-loop Bayesian optimization driving composition selection through tensile testing has been published as of late 2026. This represents a significant gap and opportunity in the field.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Camelot, a low-cost, computer-automated micro-extensometer for plant-tissue tensile and mechanical testing rather than a conventional universal testing machine. Its principal components are a force sensor with a sample attachment point, a second attachment point mounted to an actuator, and an optical camera system. The load sensor is a parallel-beam sensor of the type commonly used in digital weighing scales. Actuation is provided by a stepper motor driving a screw mechanism that moves a stage along a linear rail. Displacement or deformation is measured optically using either a compact digital microscope, a microscope camera, or cell/tissue landmarks viewed under an inverted or upright microscope. Control and integration are handled by MorphoRobotX, described as an integrated open-source software environment. The system is intended to measure elasticity, creep, yield stress, stiffness, and deformation, including stress–strain behavior in delicate plant samples. The excerpt emphasizes portability, low-cost optical tracking, and suitability for resource-limited or exploratory biomechanics work. However, these pages do not provide numerical load capacity, load-cell rating, displacement range or resolution, total build cost, or explicit compliance with ASTM E8 or ASTM D638. Therefore, the information supports only a qualitative specification and cannot establish standards compliance for metals or plastics testing.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial specifications for open-source DIY and universal testing machines, but it does not give a complete comparison of load cells, displacement sensors, costs, or ASTM compliance. Existing DIY machines commonly use wood and/or 3D-printed plastic, which restricts them to relatively low loads. They typically employ inexpensive electronics and weak motors, with operation through buttons or a connected computer. The MT-01 is a more capable open-source-style design based on aluminum profiles, a special Nema 23 stepper motor, Arduino control, linear rails, and 3D-printed parts. Its stated maximum permissible load is 1.5 kN. User interaction is provided by a momentary rocker switch and encoder, while an LCD displays test parameters and results; a USB-connected computer is required for extracting more detailed information. Commercial universal testing machines are described as expensive to purchase and maintain, requiring training and safety-related instruction. Their masses range from 55 kg to 2100 kg, and moving them generally requires recalibration. The excerpt does not specify the MT-01’s load-cell model, exact displacement-measurement method, price, or whether it complies with ASTM E8 or ASTM D638. It likewise gives no explicit standards-compliance information for the commercial machines.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the open-source MT-02 universal/material testing machine. Its design emphasizes low cost, light weight, ease of operation, and extensibility while supporting loads in the kilonewton range. The load measurement system uses a load cell rated for a maximum load of 5 kN. Crosshead actuation is provided by two NEMA 17 stepper motors, each incorporating a 19.203:1 gearbox and controlled through DM542T stepper drivers. The motors drive two SFU 1605 ball-screw assemblies with 0.5 m spindles, producing the crosshead’s vertical movement. The machine frame uses 40 mm × 80 mm aluminum profiles, with aluminum mounts and 3D-printed PETG components. Replication is supported by an open-source workflow using FreeCAD, KiCad, PrusaSlicer, Arduino IDE, and PuTTY; the PCB was manufactured externally. The excerpt does not specify the purchase or fabrication cost, the exact displacement-measurement sensor or resolution, or compliance with ASTM E8 or ASTM D638. It only states that accuracy was evaluated through tensile testing and comparison with a ZwickRoell universal testing machine.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the MT-02, an open-source universal testing machine intended for academic training and demonstrations. Its stated mechanical specification is tensile and compression testing with loads up to 3.5 kN. The machine uses a frame made from standardized aluminum profiles, while lightly loaded components are 3D printed. Control is Arduino-based, operation is through a touch display, and measurement data are transferred to a PC through USB. The excerpt indicates that displacement of the crosshead is used to estimate specimen strain; comparison with a commercial machine equipped with a video extensometer found that this estimated strain differed by a factor of two, causing Young’s modulus to be underestimated by 48%. Optical strain measurement is identified as a potential improvement. The abstract characterizes the design as affordable, portable, extendable in hardware and software, and buildable in a suitably equipped workshop with relatively low budget and effort. However, these pages do not specify the load-cell model or rating, exact construction cost, actuation mechanism, or compliance with ASTM E8 or ASTM D638. They also do not provide detailed specifications for other DIY machines; the contents indicate that component and design details appear in later sections of the thesis.
contexts.question: What are the specifications of open-source DIY tensile testing machines and universal testing machines? Including load capacity, load cell, displacement measurement, actuation method, cost, and standards compliance (ASTM E8, ASTM D638)?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the open-source MT-02 universal testing machine as a portable, extensible, moderately priced educational device capable of tensile and compression testing. It uses an Arduino-based control system, stepper motors, a TFT LCD touch screen, USB-B connectivity, and open-source software; the excerpt does not state the machine’s maximum load capacity, load-cell model or rating, total construction cost, or compliance with ASTM E8 or ASTM D638. Displacement and strain can be evaluated using crosshead travel, but this is affected by machine and clamp compliance. A video extensometer is identified as the more precise approach because it is not influenced by machine compliance; digital image correlation is also suggested as a possible displacement-tracking method. In comparisons with a ZwickRoell UTM, MT-02 stress/tensile-strength results were similar, with tensile strength only about 1% lower, while strain and Young’s modulus showed substantial discrepancies. The reported corrected MT-02 values included approximately 0.717 GPa Young’s modulus, 40.419 MPa tensile strength, 7.581% ultimate strain, and 800.346 N ultimate load. Proposed extensions include automated testing, preload application, cyclic testing, and software-only modifications to the Arduino code.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Camelot as an open-source, DIY-style micro-extensometer rather than a conventional universal testing machine. It consists of a force sensor/load cell, a linear actuator, and a camera for optical deformation tracking. The load sensors are parallel-beam sensors for single-axis measurement, available from approximately 10 g to several kilograms; the cited 10 g and 100 g models cost about £10 each, and the 10 g sensor provides approximately 10 μN resolution. Force measurement uses a Phidgets Wheatstone Bridge and amplifier. Displacement is measured optically by a camera integrated with MorphoRobotX, with overall system resolution of approximately 5 μm. Actuation uses a stepper motor driving a screw and linear rail; a 1-mm-pitch screw and 1.8° motor increments produce 5 μm movement per step, with optional subdivision. The actuator costs approximately £50. MorphoRobotX is free, open-source software running on Linux and communicating through USB. The excerpt does not state the complete assembled-system cost, maximum tensile load for a finished machine, or compliance with ASTM E8 or ASTM D638. It also provides no specifications for separate commercial universal testing machines, so standards compliance cannot be inferred.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides limited information about in-situ miniature tensile stages and does not give the requested comparative specifications, load capacities, or prices for Deben, Kammrath Weiss, Psylotech, MTI SEMtester, or Linkam TST350 systems. It identifies the Deben device as a commercial in-situ load stage used with laboratory-scale XCT and notes that such systems commonly use a stiff, X-ray-transparent PEI cylinder as the load column. The authors caution that compliance in the load frame, fixtures, grips, and non-gauge specimen regions can substantially affect crosshead-based displacement and measured elastic modulus. In their comparison, the elastic stiffness measured using the Deben system was 26 times lower than that measured with a conventional load frame for the same IN718 material, attributed in part to system compliance and displacement measurement limitations. The paper’s main contribution is a surface-strain measurement method combining laboratory XCT, 2D X-ray imaging, and particle tracking/DIC; it is not a catalog or market survey of miniature tensile stages.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the MT-02 as a simple, lightweight, inexpensive, and extendable open-source universal tensile/material testing machine designed to withstand loads in the kilonewton range. Its frame uses 40 mm × 80 mm aluminum profiles, with aluminum mounts and 3D-printed PETG components fastened using M8 screws and slot nuts. Crosshead motion is provided by two NEMA 17 stepper motors, each incorporating a 19.203:1 gearbox and controlled through DM542T stepper drivers. The vertical drive uses two SFU 1605 ball-screw assemblies with 0.5 m-long spindles. Force measurement is performed using a load cell rated for a maximum load of 5 kN. The design and fabrication used open-source software, including FreeCAD, KiCad, PrusaSlicer, Arduino IDE, and PuTTY; the PCB was the only component manufactured off-site. For validation, tensile tests were performed on the MT-02 and on a commercial ZwickRoell universal testing machine, and the results were compared to assess stress and strain precision and accuracy. The supplied pages do not provide the displacement-sensor specification or total machine cost, so those details require other sections of the article.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the open-source tensile-testing machine as the MT-02 and describes its validation methodology rather than its complete hardware specification. The MT-02 was compared with a commercial ZwickRoell RetroLine universal testing machine. Five samples were tested in each series, with samples produced simultaneously under identical 3D-printing conditions. The MT-02 determined displacement from the number of stepper-motor steps, whereas the ZwickRoell used a video extensometer tracking marks on the specimen. For MT-02 testing, the load cell was calibrated using a 0.5 kg reference weight, samples were tared before each test, and tensile tests used a 30–40 N pre-load followed by displacement-controlled motion at 1 mm/min. Time, displacement, and load were recorded through the serial port at 5 Hz. Testing stopped upon rupture or necking, identified by a sharp force decrease below 700 N after the peak load. The excerpt does not provide the machine’s load-cell rated capacity, specific stepper-motor model, lead-screw dimensions or pitch, an independent displacement sensor, total construction cost, or quantitative validation results against the ZwickRoell. contexts.context: The excerpt describes an open-source DIY electromechanical tensile testing machine (DIY EMTT) intended for stretchable conductive and soft materials. Its design integrates a displacement-sensing module, resistance/electrical tester, load cell, and linear-stage module so mechanical and electrical properties can be recorded simultaneously. The machine is rated for a maximum tensile load of 10 kg, with the load-cell and stepper-motor modules identified as the limiting components; higher loads would require replacing those modules. A VL53L0X displacement sensor interfaces with an Arduino Nano through I2C (SDA=A4, SCL=A5), while the excerpt also provides HX711 load-cell wiring and Arduino connections. The TB6560 driver supports selectable step modes and GUI speeds of 500, 200, 100, and 0.9 mm/min, with the first three associated with JIS K 6251 and/or ASTM D412 standards. The system costs several hundred dollars, compared with several thousand dollars for conventional equipment. Testing demonstrated synchronized tensile and electrical data at approximately 7 data points per second. Validation of the electrical tester and load-cell modules used a Sanwa LCR 700 and ACIS AD300H, respectively. contexts.context: The HardwareX machine is a modular, low-cost DIY electromechanical tensile tester (DIY-EMTT) integrating mechanical loading, force measurement, displacement monitoring, and electrical resistance measurement under a LabVIEW GUI. Its linear stage uses a 500 mm aluminum-profile guide rail, a Nema 23 stepper motor, and a lead screw to convert rotary motion into linear motion. A TB6560 driver supports half-, 1/8-, and 1/16-step operation, enabling slow tensile motion. Linear-stage movement is measured with a VL53L0X infrared proximity sensor rather than calculated from motor pulses; the system has a maximum displacement of 50 cm, while the sensor is generally accurate to approximately 60 cm depending on conditions. Force is measured using a low-cost 10 kg load cell connected to an HX711 amplifier/ADC, selectable at 10 or 80 Hz. The electrical tester uses an Arduino-controlled, automatically adjusted multiple-voltage-divider circuit, with reported resistance-measurement accuracy of 1–2%. The GUI records displacement, resistance, and load simultaneously, while stress and strain require conversion from raw data. This excerpt does not provide the machine’s total construction cost or validation results against a commercial tensile-testing machine; those specifications must be obtained from other sections of the article.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence that crosshead or machine displacement can be affected by machine and gripping compliance, particularly when the specimen is held only by dowel pins. Although an effectively rigid specimen produced total measured extension below 1 µm and an estimated system compliance below 0.001 µm/N, dowel-mounted tests showed a slow initial loading response, suggesting seating, slip, or fixture compliance. Fully clamped specimens reached a steady loading rate more rapidly. Such effects can distort the initial slope used to calculate elastic modulus, and the report notes wide variation in initial load-displacement slopes. The excerpt indicates that full-field optical strain measurement or an image-correlation extensometer can measure strain directly over the gauge length and therefore avoid relying solely on crosshead displacement. Load-related offsets also matter: preload or “phantom force” was approximately 2.1 ± 1.3 N, and displacement curves were corrected by subtracting displacement at the preload point. The passage does not provide a specific machine-compliance correction procedure, specimen-alignment error, bending-strain percentage, or ASTM E1012 alignment classification. It does, however, document substantial geometric uncertainty: diameter variation up to 70 µm led to an estimated 14% uncertainty in calculated stress, which would also affect modulus if stress is derived from nominal dimensions.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies important displacement-measurement accuracy limitations relevant to determining elastic modulus in bending. The LVDTs measure displacement through the loading device rather than directly on the specimen; although loading-device compliance is described as relatively small and the reading can therefore approximate midspan deflection, the measurement still includes deformation from indentation at the load point and supports. These non-specimen contributions must be separated from the bending deflection, with support indentation represented by linear and constant terms in the fitted displacement field. The study uses DIC to measure local three-dimensional specimen displacements and fit the elastic curve, providing a specimen-based alternative to load-point or crosshead displacement. The total displacement is decomposed into support indentation, shear deflection, and bending-moment deflection. Shear is expected to be substantially smaller for slender beams, but it is still a possible source of modulus error and is estimated using cross-sectional properties and Poisson’s ratio. The excerpt also states that cross-sectional area and moment of inertia may vary along the beam length, which complicates conventional uniform-specimen calculations. It does not provide information on extensometer-specific errors, ASTM E1012 alignment classifications, numerical bending-strain percentages, or a formal machine-compliance correction procedure.
contexts.question: What are the errors and accuracy problems in measuring elastic modulus from crosshead displacement versus extensometer? Machine compliance correction, specimen alignment, bending strain percentage, ASTM E1012 classification?

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several sources of error relevant to determining elastic deformation or modulus from machine displacement rather than a direct extensometer or image-based strain measurement. Crosshead/rig displacement includes machine and fixture compliance as well as specimen deformation. In the Deben in-situ rig, dowel-pin loading caused bedding-in or seating, producing a pronounced initial lead-in and obscuring the specimen’s initial elastic response; consequently, measured displacement overstated the early specimen extension. The Instron, using jaw clamping, showed a much more rapid initial load rise, illustrating the effect of loading configuration. Independent image tracking showed little measured specimen elongation during approximately the first 100 seconds, while rig displacement increased, supporting the conclusion that early displacement was largely fixture or system accommodation. The excerpt also explicitly quantifies approximately 50 µm compliance near the UTS and notes uncertainty from averaging local elongation over the full specimen length and from unsynchronised image and rig start times. Local strain measurements varied along the sample, particularly near fracture, so a single average strain can be misleading. The supplied passage begins a section on 2° specimen misalignment but does not provide its results, any bending-strain percentage, a machine-compliance correction procedure for modulus, or an ASTM E1012 classification.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies several displacement- and geometry-related error sources relevant to elastic-modulus measurement. Crosshead displacement cannot be treated as the specimen or fixture-joint displacement because the testing machine and CBT fixture deform; therefore, machine/setup compliance must be measured experimentally and corrected. In this study, compliance was determined as 2.5 μm N−1 using a much stiffer steel specimen. The excerpt does not compare crosshead displacement with an extensometer, specify an ASTM E1012 alignment classification, or quantify a direct extensometer-versus-crosshead modulus bias. For the CBT method, nonconstant curvature caused by an unsuitable effective arm-length-to-gauge-length ratio is another major accuracy problem. Ratios above 2 are recommended in the cited work, producing curvature errors below 5.7% and bending-moment errors below 0.32% for that case; smaller gauge lengths also increase edge-effect errors. Flexure hinges require a corrected effective gauge length because deformation occurs in the transition zone, and the calculated correction agreed with FEA to within 3%. The reported flexural-modulus test speed corresponds to an average strain rate of approximately 1% per minute. Specimen alignment is not explicitly discussed in this excerpt, although fixture geometry, clamping offset, and curvature control are directly relevant to alignment and bending-strain accuracy.
contexts.question: What are the errors and accuracy problems in measuring elastic modulus from crosshead displacement versus extensometer? Machine compliance correction, specimen alignment, bending strain percentage, ASTM E1012 classification?

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses errors in elastic-modulus measurements based on crosshead displacement versus an extensometer. Crosshead-derived strain must be corrected for total test-system compliance, Ctotal, and for the specimen’s effective gauge length, L*0, which accounts for the dog-bone geometry. Without these corrections, the stress–strain response and calculated Young’s modulus differ substantially from extensometer results. With both corrections applied, the crosshead-derived strain nearly matches the extensometer strain, and the modulus agrees between dog-bone and flexure-hinge specimens, despite differences in cross section and force range. The correction is based on a linear elastic relationship and is therefore valid only in the linear stress–strain region; the reported agreement extends to approximately 0.5% strain for AlMg3 and 1% for PA6. At larger, nonlinear strains, the correction formulation is not valid and would require a nonlinear strain–stress model. Stress values themselves require no such correction and remain accurate throughout the test cycle. The excerpt does not provide information about specimen alignment errors, bending-strain percentages, or ASTM E1012 classification. It does mention that numerical integration is suitable for determining effective gauge length in flexure-hinge geometries, avoiding tedious analytical derivations.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies two important sources of error when strain is inferred from crosshead or stage displacement rather than measured directly on the specimen with an extensometer. First, the test frame and loading arrangement contribute compliance: although the stage itself was described as very stiff, the dowel-based specimen location introduced compliance estimated at approximately 0.8 µm/N at strain rates of 0.1 and 0.2 mm/min. Consequently, crosshead displacement includes deformation of the loading system, so an elastic modulus calculated without machine-compliance correction can be biased, generally appearing lower than the specimen modulus. The excerpt does not provide a direct crosshead-versus-extensometer comparison or a numerical modulus error. Second, specimen misalignment introduces bending moments and offsets, causing nonuniform loading and adding bending strain to the intended axial strain. A 2° misalignment produced a different fracture mode and altered stress distribution, although the ultimate tensile strength changed only slightly (46.8 to 46.6 MPa). The passage does not quantify bending strain as a percentage and does not discuss ASTM E1012 classifications. It therefore supports qualitative concerns about compliance correction and alignment, but not a specific ASTM classification or numerical percentage error.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly addresses errors affecting elastic-modulus measurements based on crosshead displacement. With no applied load, recorded stage movement agreed well with image-tracked movement, with less than 1 µm of apparent Y-axis motion attributed to beam deflection or image drift. Under load, however, crosshead displacement includes deformation of the complete loading system—frame, load cell, grips, couplings, and specimen—not just specimen strain. Consequently, the rig can report greater displacement than the specimen actually experiences, biasing the tensile response and any modulus calculated from crosshead displacement. In the reported tests, the difference between actual/image-tracked displacement and recorded displacement increased approximately linearly with force, corresponding to about 0.8 µm/N compliance; repeated tests gave similar results. The excerpt recommends subtracting loading-train compliance from measured displacement, especially when total displacement is small, because compliance can represent a substantial fraction of the signal. It also notes that some apparent compliance may have resulted from specimen fixation using dowel pins, while a very stiff stainless-steel specimen gave a much smaller estimated system compliance (<0.001 µm/N). The excerpt does not provide information on extensometer-versus-crosshead modulus comparisons, specimen alignment, bending-strain percentages, or ASTM E1012 alignment classifications.

Crosshead motion includes both specimen elongation and deformation of the test system, expressed as ΔX = ΔL + CtotalP. Consequently, an uncorrected modulus can be substantially biased by machine, load-frame, grip, load-cell, and clamping compliance. The clamping contribution is material-dependent and increases as specimen stiffness decreases; therefore, a compliance calibrated with one material or specimen configuration may not be transferable. The correction requires an appropriate total compliance and a geometry-dependent effective gauge length L∗0, especially for specimens with variable thickness. Incorrect geometry, gauge-length assumptions, or thickness integration will introduce additional strain error. The method is also restricted to the linear elastic region and assumes uniform stress and strain over each cross section. The excerpt does not discuss specimen alignment, bending-strain percentages, extensometer accuracy, or ASTM E1012 alignment classifications, so it cannot support specific conclusions about those issues. It does, however, imply that crosshead-derived strain is less local and more setup-dependent than extensometer strain, while an extensometer measuring directly on the gauge section avoids much of the machine and grip deformation included in crosshead displacement.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies two principal accuracy problems when elastic modulus is determined from crosshead displacement rather than a directly mounted extensometer. First, crosshead displacement includes deformation from compliance in the testing machine and grips; therefore, ΔX is not equal to specimen elongation ΔL. The authors correct this using total machine/setup compliance, expressed through ΔX = ΔL + CtotalP. They note that clamping compliance is valid only within the linear stress–strain region, whereas the total compliance is characterized over the machine’s force range. Second, the specimen’s cross section varies along the gauge length, so strain is nonuniform and different segments contribute differently to total elongation. A gauge-length/geometric correction is therefore required, especially for flexure hinges. For standard dog-bone specimens, strain is measured directly with a 50 mm mechanical clip-on extensometer; flexure hinges are too short for this approach, and attached strain gauges may interfere with small or thin-walled specimens. The excerpt does not discuss specimen alignment errors, bending-strain percentage limits, or ASTM E1012 classification. Consequently, it supports discussion of compliance and nonuniform gauge geometry, but provides no basis for assigning an ASTM E1012 alignment class or quantifying bending strain.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a random combinatorial-library architecture in which many discrete particles are dispersed across a substrate, with each particle representing a distinct point in a high-dimensional composition space. contexts.context: The excerpt describes integrating self-driving-laboratory concepts with mechanical testing through a connected infrastructure combining mechanical test rigs, digital image correlation (DIC), robotic positioning, machine-learning-based crack detection, and automated data management. During fatigue crack-growth experiments, a 3D DIC system continuously generates full-field displacement and strain data, which are stored as nodemap files. This approach emphasizes closed-loop coordination among sensing, analysis, robotic motion, and test control, while producing FAIR, reusable data and improving the information-to-cost ratio. It instead provides a general framework for classifying laboratory automation. Assistive Automation (A1) automates individual synthesis or characterization steps and includes examples such as PID-controlled thermal reactors and auto-sampling mass spectrometers. Partial Automation (A2) chains multiple sequential operations using automatic pipetting robots or fixed robot arms that move samples between instruments. Conditional Automation (A3) automates complete synthesis and characterization workflows but still requires human setup, maintenance, and intervention. Higher levels involve increasingly autonomous setup, adaptation to unusual conditions, safety handling, self-calibration, cleaning, and failure detection. The literature-review introduction identifies precise robotic manipulation, orchestration of multi-step protocols across heterogeneous instruments, and experiment optimization as central challenges, but the supplied pages do not connect these concepts to tensile or compression-test equipment. contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to SPT specimen-size effects and the correlation of SPT measurements with conventional tensile properties, but it does not specifically address EN 10371 miniature specimen dimensions or additive-manufactured metals. It states that the thickness-to-grain-size ratio (t/d) can affect whether SPT results represent bulk behavior: ratios below 25, associated with relatively large grains, may produce unrepresentative mechanical performance because of limited geometrically necessary dislocations and low-strain substructural effects. For the tested steels, t/d ratios were 45.5–74.1 for EN8 and 45.1–59.4 for EN3B, so the authors considered the results representative of the bulk material. The paper correlates SPT force-displacement parameters with tensile yield strength (YS) and ultimate tensile strength (UTS). Specifically, YS is derived from the elastic-plastic transition force Fe using a material-dependent empirical constant, while UTS is derived from maximum force Fm, initial specimen thickness h0, and displacement at maximum force um using another empirical constant. Baseline tensile testing used ASTM E8 sub-sized dog-bone specimens with an 8 mm outer diameter, 4 mm reduced diameter, and 16 mm gauge length. The measured tensile strengths were 289.04 MPa YS and 573.58 MPa UTS for EN8, and 413.37 MPa YS and 719.44 MPa UTS for EN3B.

The standard specimen is a circular miniature sample with an 8 ± 0.1 mm diameter and an initial thickness of 0.5 ± 0.005 mm; the fixture includes a Φ4 mm lower-die diameter and a punch with a 1.25 mm chamfer radius. Yield strength is estimated from the elastic-plastic transition force Fe using a relation proportional to Fe divided by the square of the initial thickness, with the force determined by bilinear or trilinear fitting of the force-displacement response. Ultimate tensile strength can be estimated from the maximum force Fm and maximum deflection um, or from the intersecting force Fi associated with plastic instability. The excerpt reports EN 10371:2021 best-fit constants βy = 0.510, βum = 0.2784, and βui = 0.1828 for steels with yield strengths between 200 and 1000 MPa. These correlations are empirical and sensitive to material-dependent constants. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the apparatus as a single-leadscrew, 2 kN Deben in-situ tensile-testing rig used inside an SEM to deform additive layer manufacturing (ALM) samples while tracking movements by image analysis. It does not provide a complete manufacturer specification sheet or an explicit stage displacement-resolution value. The reported displacement-related values are measurement findings rather than necessarily hardware specifications: unloaded stage motion agreed well with image-tracked motion, with less than 1 µm apparent Y-axis movement attributable to beam deflection or image drift. Under load, the rig’s recorded jaw displacement included deformation of the loading system—frame, load cell, grips, couplings, and specimen—so it could exceed the specimen or jaw motion measured from images. For the tested setup, the apparent compliance was approximately 0.8 µm/N, although the authors note that dowel-pin sample fixing may have contributed substantially. A very stiff stainless-steel specimen produced compliance below 0.001 µm/N in the described tests. The NPL report therefore concerns uncertainties in in-situ micromechanical testing of ALM materials, especially displacement accuracy, image tracking, acquisition timing, loading effects, and machine-compliance correction. Accurate specimen displacement requires subtracting loading-train compliance from the rig’s total measured displacement.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not identify or describe the Deben in-situ tensile testing stage, so it provides no load-capacity, displacement-resolution, or other Deben-specific specifications. It does establish the broader testing context: in-situ micromechanical testing is performed within a scanning electron microscope to observe material behavior under load, particularly in additive layer manufacturing (ALM) materials. The NPL Report MAT 128 investigates the accuracy and reliability of these measurements, concentrating on uncertainty from displacement measurement, load measurement, and specimen alignment. It notes that measurement accuracy can be affected by the SEM micromechanical stage’s resolution and calibration, as well as force-sensor and displacement-actuator precision. Misalignment can produce non-uniform stress distributions and influence measured strain, stress, modulus, maximum elongation, and tensile strength. The report uses fine-scale ALM lattice structures and individual lattice/ligament tensile specimens to illustrate these issues. Although SEM-related effects such as charging and localized heating are discussed as possible challenges, the report explicitly focuses its analysis on displacement, load, and alignment rather than SEM-environment effects. Deben stage specifications would need to be obtained from later report pages or an external Deben product source.

It identifies displacement and load measurements, and sample alignment as the primary uncertainty sources.
The primary sources of uncertainties in in-situ micromechanical testing arise from displacement and load measurements, sample alignment, and the inherent limitations of the SEM environment.
This report considers the factors affecting the accuracy of results from in-situ micromechanical testing of additive layer manufacturing (ALM) materials.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the Deben in-situ tensile stage as a miniature mechanical testing rig used inside an imaging system, with tensile load and displacement recorded while SEM images are acquired. The setup loads lattice specimens using dowel pins; this introduces an initial “lead-in” or bedding-in displacement that is not seen to the same extent when specimens are clamped in an Instron test frame. The rig was validated by comparing its load–displacement results with an Instron 5969 equipped with a 50 kN load cell. For samples containing five and two unit cells, peak loads differed by only ±0.8 N between systems; the single-cell comparison differed by approximately 4.6 ± 2.2 N. The supplied load cell is specified in the excerpt only by its accuracy, ±0.1% of full scale. Figure labels indicate Deben configurations designated 1 N, 2 N, and 5 N, but the excerpt does not provide a complete stage datasheet, explicit displacement resolution, travel range, dimensions, or a definitive load-capacity specification. The NPL report concerns uncertainty in in-situ micromechanical testing of additive-layer-manufactured materials, including load-cell accuracy versus repeatability, sample-to-sample variation, alignment, fixture compliance, image-based strain measurement, and comparison with conventional testing.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the Deben MT2000EH as a miniature, single-leadscrew mechanical testing rig used for in-situ observation inside a Thermo Fisher Apreo SEM. It supports tensile, compression, and horizontal bending tests and can be used with SEM, optical microscopy, AFM, or XRD systems. Samples are mounted horizontally on stainless-steel slide bearings and gripped with 3.25 mm diameter tool-steel rods. Its stated load capacity is provided by a miniature 2 kN load cell, which was calibrated by the supplier before delivery. The excerpt does not state a formal displacement resolution specification for the stage. Instead, it evaluates displacement accuracy and irregularities using a calibrated displacement setup block and SEM image tracking with Fiji/ImageJ SIFT alignment. Tests used crosshead speeds of 0.1 or 0.2 mm/min. The measured absolute elongation differences were typically -0.75/+0.25 µm at 0.1 mm/min and approximately ±0.5 µm at 0.2 mm/min, with larger deviations associated with abrupt loading changes. The NPL report concerns uncertainties in in-situ micromechanical testing of additive layer manufacturing materials, including specimen design, stage displacement measurement, imaging-based strain measurement, loading-rate effects, compliance, alignment, gripping, and other factors affecting measurement reliability.

contexts.context: The excerpt is from the NPL Report MAT 128, which investigates uncertainties in in-situ micromechanical tensile testing of additive layer manufacturing (ALM) materials. It discusses load and displacement measurement, fixture compliance, preload, stress calculation, dimensional variation, porosity, stress relaxation, and load-cell accuracy. Tests used a calibrated 2 kN load cell; the measured preload (phantom force) was approximately 2.1 ± 1.3 N, and the supplied load cell was certified to ±0.1% of full scale. Tests on an effectively infinitely stiff specimen indicated system compliance below 0.001 µm/N, although dowel-pin mounting produced slow and variable initial loading behavior compared with fully clamped mounting. Optical diameter variations of up to 70 µm, surface asperities, nonuniform cross-sections, and internal porosity introduced substantial uncertainty into calculated stress, estimated at approximately 14%. The excerpt does not identify the Deben in-situ tensile testing stage by name and does not provide its displacement resolution or a complete list of stage specifications. Therefore, those specific Deben parameters cannot be established from the supplied pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not identify or describe an autonomous laboratory named Ada, nor does it specify which mechanical tests Ada includes. It does provide general information about how additive manufacturing can be integrated into a closed-loop materials-discovery workflow. Self-driving laboratories combine robotic manipulation, synthesis or processing equipment, automated or in-line characterisation, sensors, and software orchestration. For metallurgy, Lawrence Livermore’s APEX is given as an example: it integrates Directed-Energy Deposition (DED) metal additive manufacturing with automated post-processing, robotic handling, and characterisation. This enables rapid iteration through composition–process–property loops, where materials are fabricated, processed, measured, and used to guide subsequent experiments. The broader architecture is described as a closed-loop Design–Make–Test–Learn system, with an AI planner orchestrating robotic synthesis and automated characterisation. The excerpt also lists mechanical testing among possible laboratory sensor functions, but does not name specific mechanical tests such as tensile, compression, hardness, or fatigue testing, and does not establish that any particular tests are included in Ada.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not identify a laboratory named Ada; it describes LLNL and Cornell’s Autonomous Alloy Prediction and EXperimentation (APEX) platform. APEX is intended as a self-driving laboratory that uses robotics, machine learning, and physics-based models to autonomously design, fabricate, prepare, and test novel alloys. Its mechanical and materials characterization includes microscopic surface examination, diamond indentation to measure hardness, and crushing samples to evaluate compression response. The platform integrates additive manufacturing into a closed-loop discovery process by selecting an alloy composition, then producing samples layer by layer through directed-energy deposition, a laser-based metal 3D-printing method that melts and fuses powder onto a substrate. Automated grinding and polishing prepare the printed samples for characterization; the system is designed to process multiple samples and potentially produce up to 48 per day. Characterization and process data are collected throughout fabrication, surface preparation, and testing, creating a complete history for each sample. These data are fed into the Materials Acceleration Platform (MAP), where algorithms and machine-learning tools use prior results to design and improve subsequent alloy samples, thereby closing the loop between computational design, automated manufacturing, and experimental evaluation.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a robot-assisted, DIC-based fatigue crack growth testing infrastructure. It combines global three-dimensional digital image correlation (3D DIC) with local, high-resolution two-dimensional DIC (2D HRDIC), providing continuous displacement and strain measurements throughout the experiment at two length scales. The infrastructure is intended to automate fatigue crack growth experiments and generate considerably more information than the conventional ASTM-based approach. DIC images are used to calculate fracture-mechanics quantities—including stress-intensity factors, mode-II loading, T-stress, and higher-order Williams-expansion terms—from experimentally measured displacement and strain fields rather than relying solely on crack length, applied load, specimen geometry, or idealized finite-element assumptions. The excerpt states that the test procedure is almost completely automated, although an individual experiment took approximately one week compared with one to two days for the conventional method. It also emphasizes the large resulting data volume, exceeding 100 GB per experiment, and the need for structured, FAIR-oriented storage and metadata. While the passage clearly supports robot-assisted DIC positioning and automated fatigue testing, it does not explicitly use the term “cobot” or provide detailed mechanical specifications of the robotic integration.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an automated, data-centric fatigue crack growth infrastructure combining a uniaxial fatigue test rig, full-field 3D digital image correlation (DIC), a robot/cobot-mounted light optical microscope for high-resolution DIC (HRDIC), convolutional neural networks, and the CrackPy open-source Python package. The primary DIC system continuously produces displacement and strain fields during fatigue testing, which are stored as node-wise “nodemap” files. CNNs automatically detect the fatigue crack path and crack-tip position from these fields, either in situ or after the experiment. In situ crack-tip information can be sent to the DIC system, robot, and test-rig controller, enabling coordinated automation. The cobot positions the microscope at a crack-tip-centered region of interest or scans the specimen surface in a checkerboard pattern. Automated fine adjustment of the robot position keeps the selected region in focus. Thus, the setup integrates fatigue-test control, robotic microscope positioning, multiscale DIC acquisition, automated crack detection, and algorithmic data management. The excerpt specifically states that the hardware was fully automated for uniaxial test rigs; it also notes that the system had recently been adapted for biaxial testing, although the provided text ends before describing that adaptation in detail.

DIC is integrated with digital twins, IoT-supported diagnostics, and deep-learning computer-vision models, specifically YOLOv7 and DeepLabv3+, to track crack growth in near real time. The reported system exceeds 95% accuracy and converts strain maps into automated diagnostic outputs, reducing reliance on manual visual inspection. For tests where optical access is obstructed, path-integrated X-ray DIC uses synthetic reference images to measure displacement of moving internal layers, including in high-temperature build chambers. Real-time DIC feedback also supports sensitivity-based adjustment of noise effects during inverse material-parameter identification. More broadly, the article presents this combination as physics-informed autonomous metrology aimed at zero-defect manufacturing and reduced human intervention. contexts.context: The excerpt describes an automated experimental-mechanics infrastructure combining robotic optical measurement, fatigue testing, and software-based analysis. A collaborative robot (cobot) carries a light optical microscope (LOM), enabling high-magnification DIC/HRDIC measurements. The robot can position the microscope at a crack-tip region identified from crack information or scan the specimen surface in a checkerboard pattern. Its position is fine-adjusted automatically to ensure sharp focus. The hardware is fully automated for uniaxial test rigs and has also been adapted to a biaxial rig. For the reported fatigue experiment, this robot-based infrastructure was integrated into a servo-hydraulic uniaxial test machine applying a sinusoidal cyclic load at 20 Hz, from 4.5 to 15 kN (R = 0.3). CrackPy automates the subsequent data workflow: DIC data and metadata are stored in structured formats, crack tips can be detected using trained convolutional neural networks, and fracture parameters such as energy release rates, stress-intensity factors, T-Stress, and higher-order Williams-series terms are calculated. The resulting structured datasets support automated, data-centric analysis and future machine-learning or symbolic-regression workflows.

contexts.context: The automated test infrastructure combines a standard uniaxial fatigue-testing rig with global and robot-assisted high-resolution digital image correlation (DIC), robotics, and the CrackPy software framework. Global 3D DIC was performed using a commercial GOM Aramis 12M system and Aramis Professional 2021, while CrackPy captured metadata, controlled the experiment, performed on-the-fly crack detection, and stored displacement and strain results in human-readable files. For local measurements, a KUKA LBR iiwa collaborative robot carries a Zeiss STEMI 206C optical microscope fitted with a Basler global-shutter CMOS camera. The robot is used to position the microscope over regions of interest and acquire high-resolution images around the crack tip. Crack detection is automated using trained convolutional neural networks—ParallelNets for crack-tip detection and UNetPath for crack-path detection—using global DIC displacement fields as input. During fatigue testing, DCPD measurements following ASTM E-647 control crack-length progression. The test is paused at each 0.5 mm of crack extension; the system identifies the crack-tip region and automatically moves the robot to the relevant reference-image positions to capture images at multiple load conditions. This creates an integrated, largely automated infrastructure for fatigue crack-growth experiments.

Question: I am evaluating low-cost / open-source / DIY mechanical test frames (tensile and compression testers, universal testing machines, UTMs) for use in an autonomous self-driving laboratory that does high-throughput metallurgy and 3D-printed materials research. I need a survey of the MOST RECENT designs, with emphasis on 2024, 2025 and 2026 publications and releases, because earlier searches (done in early 2025) may have missed newer work.

Please find and describe, with citations and URLs wherever possible:

1. Open-source / open-hardware tensile and compression testing machines published in HardwareX, Journal of Open Hardware, PLOS ONE, Rapid Prototyping Journal, Review of Scientific Instruments, Machines, Inventions, SoftwareX, or similar venues, especially 2024-2026. For each, report: maximum load capacity (N or kN), load cell type and resolution, crosshead displacement measurement method and resolution, actuation (stepper + lead screw, linear actuator, servo, hydraulic), frame stiffness/compliance handling, total bill-of-materials cost, standards compliance (ASTM E8/E8M for metals, ASTM D638 for plastics, ISO 6892-1), and whether the design is validated against a commercial load frame.

2. In-situ / miniature tensile stages designed for use inside a scanning electron microscope (SEM), under an optical microscope, on an X-ray diffractometer, or for digital image correlation (DIC). Especially designs with symmetric / dual opposed lead screws that keep the gauge section stationary during the test. Include commercial examples (Deben Microtest, Kammrath & Weiss, Psylotech, MTI Instruments SEMtester, Admet, Linkam TST350, Alemnis, Bruker/Hysitron PI series, FemtoTools) with approximate load capacities and price bands if available, and any open-source equivalents.

3. Designs specifically aimed at small / sub-size / micro tensile specimens, including miniature specimen test technique (MSTT), small punch test (SPT/EN 10371), and sub-size ASTM E8 specimens, for additively manufactured metals. Discuss how specimen miniaturization affects the measured properties and what gauge lengths and load ranges are typical.

4. Automated, robot-compatible, or self-driving-laboratory-integrated mechanical testing: autosamplers, robotic specimen handling into load frames, closed-loop Bayesian-optimization-driven mechanical property optimization, and any published SDL that includes a tensile or compression test as the characterization step. Include high-throughput mechanical screening approaches (nanoindentation mapping, high-throughput micro-tensile arrays, combinatorial libraries) as alternatives.

5. Practical guidance on the main accuracy pitfalls of small/DIY load frames: specimen bending and misalignment (bending strain as a percentage, ASTM E1012 classification of alignment), machine compliance corrections to extract true elastic modulus, grip slippage, load cell drift and calibration, and why extensometry or DIC is usually required rather than crosshead displacement for modulus measurement. Quantify typical errors where the literature gives numbers.

Please prioritize recent (2024-2026) primary sources, give concrete numbers, and provide direct links (DOIs, GitHub repos, project pages) so I can follow up.

# Survey of Low-Cost, Open-Source, and DIY Mechanical Test Frames for Autonomous Self-Driving Laboratories in Metallurgy and 3D-Printed Materials Research

## 1. Open-Source / Open-Hardware Tensile and Compression Testing Machines

Several recent open-source mechanical testing designs have been documented, though none yet demonstrate full standards compliance for metals testing (ASTM E8/E8M or ISO 6892-1).

**MT-02 (Demmel, 2024, TU Wien).** This is the most capable recent open-source UTM identified. It uses a 40×80 mm aluminum profile frame, two NEMA 17 stepper motors with 19.203:1 gearboxes driving twin SFU 1605 ball-screw assemblies (500 mm spindles), and a 5 kN load cell. The controller is Arduino-based with a touchscreen display. The rated load capacity is 3.5 kN. Displacement is inferred from motor steps at 5 Hz logging. Testing is displacement-controlled at speeds such as 1 mm/min, with 30–40 N preload. Crucially, validation against a ZwickRoell RetroLine with video extensometer showed that tensile strength agreed within ~1%, but the crosshead-derived strain differed by approximately a factor of two, causing a **48% underestimate of Young's modulus** (demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 1-6, demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 64-68). The design is open-source using FreeCAD, KiCad, PrusaSlicer, and Arduino IDE, though the total BOM cost was not explicitly stated (demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 25-30). It references DIN 50125 and ISO 527-1 specimen geometries but does not claim ASTM E8 or D638 compliance (demmel2024designmanufacturingand pages 13-17).

**DIY-EMTT (Wiranata et al., 2024, HardwareX).** This modular design targets stretchable/soft materials. It integrates a NEMA 23 stepper motor with TB6560 driver on a 500 mm aluminum linear stage, a 10 kg (≈98 N) load cell with HX711 amplifier, a VL53L0X time-of-flight displacement sensor, and a built-in resistance meter for simultaneous electromechanical testing. Four Arduino Nano boards coordinate with a LabVIEW GUI. The stated BOM cost is **US$173.28**, and designs are released under CC BY-SA 4.0 via a Mendeley Data repository. GUI speeds of 500, 200, and 100 mm/min are associated with JIS K 6251 / ASTM D412 standards for elastomers, but ASTM E8 or D638 compliance is not demonstrated (wiranata2024economicallyviableelectromechanical pages 9-11, wiranata2024economicallyviableelectromechanical pages 3-6, wiranata2024economicallyviableelectromechanical pages 1-3).

**Camelot Micro-Extensometer (Trozzi et al., 2025, BMC Biology).** This is a low-cost system designed for plant biomechanics rather than engineering materials, but its architecture is instructive. It uses interchangeable parallel-beam load sensors (from ~10 g to several kg capacity, ≈£10 each; the 10 g sensor provides ~10 µN resolution), a stepper motor with a 1 mm pitch screw producing 5 µm steps, and camera-based optical tracking providing ~5 µm displacement resolution. The actuator costs approximately £50. The open-source MorphoRobotX software runs on Linux (trozzi2025camelotacomputerautomated pages 2-4, trozzi2025camelotacomputerautomated pages 1-2).

**Arduino UTM (Geasa, 2021).** A minimal design using a steel frame, NEMA 23 stepper motor (19 kg·cm torque, 1.8° step angle), TB6600 driver, lead-screw actuator, and a load cell with Arduino logging. Total cost was below 1,000 Egyptian pounds (approximately US$20–30 at the time). Displacement is controlled through motor steps with no independent sensor (geasa2021developmentofan pages 1-3).

An additional notable design is the **open-source flexible material tensile testing apparatus by Woods et al. (2024)** published in the journal *Hardware* (DOI: 10.3390/hardware2010002), though full details could not be retrieved in this search.
